chunks.content: se of this article is to describe the rationale, components and advantages of an updated dental anatomy module and present a comparison of student course evaluations for those who received the updated module (CDM) versus those who received the traditional module (TM). Method: An updated module was implemented at the University of Kentucky College of Dentistry (UKCD). The updated module consisted of clinically based lectures and incorporated digital technologies in both lecture and laboratory portions of the course as well as a patient-based aesthetic wax-up exercise. The goal of the updated module is to shift emphasis away from decontextualised technical learning towards more active and clinically applicable learning that improves classroom interaction and takes advantage of the current technologies available. Results: The results were statistically analysed using a two-sample t test. The up - dated module was statistically significantly highly rated by students. Conclusion: The

An update to the educational method of teaching dental anatomy and morphology is proposed, clinical dental anatomy teaching results in enhanced students’ engagement and assessment. These books are the primary resources used by the students and by most dental schools. Instructors pre - pare their lectures, with the intention of highlighting important an - atomical information that are necessary for the student dentist to be able to restore and replace teeth as well as recognise and diag - nose different oral conditions. Influenced by the textbook lay-out, the final product mostly becomes a summarised version of these books with minimal clinical relevance. The traditional dental anat - omy teaching model presents several limitations, including one-way communication, lack of interaction and poor student engagement. 3 As one of the first courses directly related to teeth and oral function, dental anatomy has a special status in the pre-clinical curriculum; first year students are usually eager to learn the material; however, this is often met with

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: tly related to teeth and oral function, dental anatomy has a special status in the pre-clinical curriculum; first year students are usually eager to learn the material; however, this is often met with disappointment as students struggle to associ - ate tooth morphology with clinical dentistry and they feel the course does not meet their expectations, the subject is often described as “boring” and the students loose the opportunity of what can be a great learning experience. 3 This problem is identified in the litera - ture as “decontextualised technical learning”. 4 Dental anatomy learning at the University of Kentucky College of Dentistry (UKCD) remained unchanged for several years and fol - lowed the traditional teaching methods, the same holds true in most dental schools and in many different countries. 4 UKCD has recently incorporated the use of digital technology, and it has become one of the school's goals to prepare future dentists in becoming profi - cient in digital dentistry

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: fferent countries. 4 UKCD has recently incorporated the use of digital technology, and it has become one of the school's goals to prepare future dentists in becoming profi - cient in digital dentistry which has become an integral part of to - day's dentistry. The lack of introducing this technology in the dental curriculum may negatively affect future generations of dentists as the use of this technology is gradually taking over the market with the possible need for graduates to seek additional resources to learn digitally related techniques if these methods were not introduced as an integral part of the dental curriculum. In addition, this technol - ogy offers several advantages such as: teaching oral anatomy using digital interactive dental models, digital evaluation and feedback which are generated based on comparison of scanned student work to a scanned gold standard, digital treatment planning and providing high-quality fast-paced patient care as indirect restorations can be

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: hich are generated based on comparison of scanned student work to a scanned gold standard, digital treatment planning and providing high-quality fast-paced patient care as indirect restorations can be fabricated without the need for conventional impressions and in - creased laboratory wait times. As part of the efforts of the restorative dentistry division at UKCD in improving the students’ educational experience, the dental anatomy module was updated with the goal of creating a clinically based course, which relates tooth morphology to clinical-based sce - narios and incorporates the use of digital technology. The purpose of this article is to describe this new approach to teaching dental anatomy and compare students’ course evaluations who received the updated module or the clinical- and digital-based module (CDM) to those who received the traditional module (TM). We hypothe - sised that the updated module would facilitate the process of learn - ing dental anatomy and improve the

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: and digital-based module (CDM) to those who received the traditional module (TM). We hypothe - sised that the updated module would facilitate the process of learn - ing dental anatomy and improve the overall student satisfaction and educational experience. 2 | METHOD The study was determined to be a non-human subject research project by the medical institution review board UKCD. In 2016, the dental anatomy course was taught to first year dental students in their first semester in its traditional manners which consisted of presenting detailed textbook style anatomical description of tooth anatomy during lecture, followed by laboratory practice sessions for different waxing exercises. The laboratory projects were comprised of 5 partial crown wax-ups, 6 full crown wax-ups, 2 waxing in occlu - sion projects as well as a die-trimming exercise. These projects were done over a 5-month period in 90 hours including practical exami - nations. The author performed a comprehensive curriculum

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: cclu - sion projects as well as a die-trimming exercise. These projects were done over a 5-month period in 90 hours including practical exami - nations. The author performed a comprehensive curriculum update to both the lecture and laboratory components of the course, and the final updated module was implemented in the fall of 2018. The lectures were updated to incorporate a clinically relevant teaching style and patient-based content as well as an interactive three-di - mensional tooth viewing software. The laboratory component was updated to incorporate a comprehensive instruction manual with video demonstrations, digital scanning and the use of a digital evalu - ation software as well as a patient-based scenario aesthetic wax-up exercise. The number of waxing projects was reduced to 3 partial wax-ups, 5 full crown wax-ups, 1 waxing in occlusion project and the die-trimming exercise was moved to a different course. 2.1 | Clinically relevant dental anatomy lectures The individual

These features were introduced to the students through patient-based cases with photographs and/or videos. An example is the maxillary central incisor, this is the first tooth the students learn about, the first slide in the presentation states the clinically relevant features about a maxillary central incisor as follows: (a) the most prominent teeth aesthetically, (b) the most prone to trauma and (c) having a straight conical root. The first unique feature is explained further to the students by showing photographs of patients with discol - oured or mal-aligned central incisors before and after treatment. For the second unique feature, the tooth position in the centre of the mouth and the tooth angulation are discussed and a 2-minute video is displayed showing sport-related injuries to the tooth. The third unique feature is also explained via a short video of a max - illary central incisor extraction through rotation which is possible given its conical root. Students in both groups TM & CDM received the surveys immediately upon course completion. 3 | RESULTS Class of 2016 who received TM consisted of 68 students (M: 36, F: 32) and class of 2018 who received CDM consisted of 65 students (M: 27, F: 38).The response rate for students who received TM was 88.2% vs 81.5% for students who received CDM. The results were statistically analysed using a two-sample t test. The updated module was statistically significantly highly rated by students in all 7 disci - plines (Table 1). 4 | DISCUSSION Learning dental anatomy in a descriptive mode is often extremely detailed, overwhelming and challenging to recall. As such; tradi - tional dental anatomy learning does little to prepare students for the transition from pre-patient care to patient care. 2-4 In 2016 when the traditional module was implemented, the course was rated low by students with

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: my learning does little to prepare students for the transition from pre-patient care to patient care. 2-4 In 2016 when the traditional module was implemented, the course was rated low by students with average scores ranging between 2.5 and 2.8 for the different disciplines evaluated (Table 1). This coincided with the school's goal to incorporate digital dentistry in pre-clinical courses; these were the motives behind performing the module update. The updated module aims at early preparation of students for restoration of teeth in an anatomical fashion and encourages them to realise the link between tooth morphology learning and clinical restora - tive dentistry. An additional aim of the updated module was to in - troduce students to digital technologies available similar to those used in a restorative clinical-based setting. By achieving those aims, dental anatomy learning is expected to align better with the fol - lowing CODA standards; 2-24—at a minimum, graduates must be competent

chunks.content: a restorative clinical-based setting. By achieving those aims, dental anatomy learning is expected to align better with the fol - lowing CODA standards; 2-24—at a minimum, graduates must be competent in providing oral health care within the scope of general dentistry, as defined by the school, including: 2-24 f—restoration of teeth, 2-24 h—replacement of teeth including fixed, removable and dental implant prosthodontic therapies. 7 Based on the results of this study, our hypothesis was accepted; the new module resulted in greater student satisfaction as apparent by the results of the course evaluation. In 2018, the course was rated highly by students with average scores ranging between 3.5 and 3.7 for the different disci - plines evaluated (Table 1). In our study, we combined two concepts: clinical-based dental anatomy teaching and the incorporation of digital dentistry. chunks.content: | 657 ABDALLA et AL. be taught in many different ways: traditional teaching or text - book style teaching has been proven to be relevantly poor. 2,7 A link must be created between course objectives and the teaching style which will maximise student's satisfaction and improve their educational experience. Utilising every beneficial resource and constantly looking for additional resources is the responsibility of dental educators. In the updated module, new clinically relevant dental anatomy lectures were introduced. A problem-based learning approach was adopted which enables students to correlate basic knowledge with clinical scenarios. This approach allows vertical and horizontal inte - gration of knowledge and leads to better results. 2,8 Keiser et al in 2008 introduced a professional story telling clinical dental anatomy teaching method as a part of their problem-based learning approach. In their study, a 37.5% higher student satisfaction was found for the group that received

chunks.content: onal story telling clinical dental anatomy teaching method as a part of their problem-based learning approach. In their study, a 37.5% higher student satisfaction was found for the group that received stories vs students without stories. 8 Magne in 2015 redesigned the dental morphology and occlusion module by introducing 2D-3D & 4D concepts. His approach focused on visual arts and starts with 2D drawings of teeth followed by performing 3D partial and full wax-ups of teeth including an aesthetic wax-up exer - cise. The concept of 4D was introduced with concepts of histoanat - omy of enamel and dentine replicated using layered acrylic mock-ups and resin restoration materials. The author reports increased stu - dent and staff satisfaction with the redesigned module and antic - ipated that it will help students develop deep clinical appreciation for dental morphology, function and aesthetics. 4 Bakr et al in 2016 introduced a flipped classroom method of teaching dental anatomy to improve

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: t will help students develop deep clinical appreciation for dental morphology, function and aesthetics. 4 Bakr et al in 2016 introduced a flipped classroom method of teaching dental anatomy to improve student's engagement. In their method, an online digital library and online quizzes for self-reflected learning were developed as well as a series of online videos demonstrating different practi - cal tasks such as wax carving and tooth identification. A significant improvement was found in students’ performance in practical ex - aminations as well as the course evaluations when compared to the traditional teaching method implemented the years before. 9 Obrez et al in 2011 introduced a revised dental anatomy module to improve cognitive and psychomotor skill development of dental students. In their study, didactic lectures and tooth morphology practicals were replaced with a new curriculum consisting of digitised material, small- group discussions between the instructor and students and a

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: their study, didactic lectures and tooth morphology practicals were replaced with a new curriculum consisting of digitised material, small- group discussions between the instructor and students and a labora - tory exercise developed around the clinical application of restoring the teeth. Their results showed no statistical difference in cognitive learning as evaluated by final written examinations and objective structured clinical examination. However, there was a statistically significant increase in students’ psychomotor skill development and performance as evaluated by their final tooth waxing project. 2 An integral part of the updated module was the incorporation of a comprehensive instruction manual and video demonstrations uploaded on YouTube. The manual included an introduction to wax - ing techniques, introductory waxing exercises and full crown wax- ups. The aim of creating this manual was to have a comprehensive resource for the laboratory course that includes all the

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: ion to wax - ing techniques, introductory waxing exercises and full crown wax- ups. The aim of creating this manual was to have a comprehensive resource for the laboratory course that includes all the information needed to easily reproduce tooth anatomy using wax and eliminate the students' need for seeking additional resources. The fundamental steps of waxing teeth were essentially the same for each project; however, certain differences exist depending on the tooth type and the requirements for each project. Reduced number of projects al - lowed students to focus on quality work and provided time to in - corporate the additional aspects of the updated module. Magne in 2015 in his redesigned course incorporated detailed manuals and in - structional videos to accompany each laboratory session. His videos however were uploaded on the school's blackboard learning website rather than YouTube. 4 Educational videos uploaded on YouTube are being utilised widely to teach dental students. 10

His videos however were uploaded on the school's blackboard learning website rather than YouTube. 4 Educational videos uploaded on YouTube are being utilised widely to teach dental students. 10 Turkyilmaz et al in 2019 conducted a survey to evaluate New York University (NYU) dental student perceptions of the influence of online applications and animations on their perceived academic performance. Their re- sults show the most commonly used application was YouTube, which seems ideal for visual learning. 11 This finding is similar to findings from other studies by Knosel et al in 2011 and Duncan et al in 2012 who concluded that YouTube is a valuable medium offering several educational opportunities. 12,13 Uploading video demonstrations on YouTube can thus be used as a valuable tool to reach out to den - tal students through a preferred medium. The advantage of video demonstrations as compared to an instructor demonstrating live for students is that students are able to watch the

chunks.content: to reach out to den - tal students through a preferred medium. The advantage of video demonstrations as compared to an instructor demonstrating live for students is that students are able to watch the videos more than once and have the freedom and flexibility to watch the videos at their own pace. 4 The availability of a three-dimensional software such as tooth explorer™ used in this study offers the advantage of a highly effi - cient teaching environment with motivational features that make the discipline fun to learn and engaging for students. 6 Students are able to engage in self-paced learning by rotating and identifying sig - nificant features of individual, anatomically correct teeth. Similarly, Bogacki et al in 2004 conducted a randomised controlled study, testing the efficacy of a computer-assisted learning program “Tooth Morphology” against traditional lectures. This study was conducted in a cohort of first year dental students at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) and

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: f a computer-assisted learning program “Tooth Morphology” against traditional lectures. This study was conducted in a cohort of first year dental students at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) and concluded that “Tooth Morphology” program was statistically equivalent to traditional lectures as measured by ex - aminations. However, many advantages of using the program were realised including: greater student-faculty interaction, greater stu - dent control over pace, more time for faculty to help struggling stu - dents and introduce clinical relevance, less time maintaining course materials and less expense. This has led to using “Tooth Morphology” in combination with interactive class meetings as a replacement to the traditional dental anatomy lectures at VCU. 14 Recent studies in the literature have investigated the useful - ness, accuracy and reproducibility of the use of intraoral scanning in conjunction with the E4D compare software as follows: Lam et al in 2015 concluded that

chunks.content: 658 | ABDALLA et AL. of digital technology in dental anatomy grading. 17 Additionally; Lam et al in 2015 found a strong correlation between visual and digital scores which supports the validity of the use of digital technology in assessing students’ projects and suggests that this tool could also be used for official grading in competencies as high grades were con - sistently graded as high and low grades as low across the two meth - ods. 15 In contrast to these supportive studies, Kwon et al in 2015 suggested that the implementation of digital technology in the con - text of an existing dental anatomy course did not enhance students’ technical performance and self-evaluation skills. The results of their study showed that the majority of students did not appreciate im - plementation of the digital systems. Students were given a survey to rate their experience with digital scanning and the use of E4D and were found to be nearly split on their sentiments regarding the difficulties in

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: the digital systems. Students were given a survey to rate their experience with digital scanning and the use of E4D and were found to be nearly split on their sentiments regarding the difficulties in learning and completing a digital evaluation. The least favourable responses were to the question of whether the tech - nologies should be incorporated into the curriculum. However, the authors reported these results could be attributed to non-strategic integration of digital softwares into the curriculum. 18 Smile design has become a very popular practice in dentistry es - pecially with the advancement in ceramics in the recent decades, which makes it crucial to introduce dental students to the princi - ples of aesthetics as early as possible to be able to comply with this practice. 5 Therefore, as a part of the updated module, students were required to complete an aesthetic wax-up on a cast according to a patient profile of their choice. Aesthetic wax-ups are indicated when anterior

chunks.book_title: Eur J Dental Education - 2020 - Abdalla - Teaching dental anatomy   morphology  An updated clinical‐   digital‐based
chunks.content: erefore, as a part of the updated module, students were required to complete an aesthetic wax-up on a cast according to a patient profile of their choice. Aesthetic wax-ups are indicated when anterior restorations are planned to restore carious lesions, fractures, wear, diastema closures, intrinsic discoloration, micro- dontia which most commonly affect the lateral incisors (peg shaped lateral) or to enhance a poor smile. 19 Students were given the free - dom to create different looking smiles with different line and point angles/embrasures and teeth lengths according to what suits their pre-chosen patients’ profile. The main requirement in this exercise was to create mirror-shaped contralateral teeth and an anatomical harmonious smile. Fabricating an aesthetic wax-up is an excellent learning exercise that allows students to realise the importance of learning and perfecting the details of anterior teeth morphology and its effect on the appearance of a smile. Failure to relate anterior

chunks.content: ning exercise that allows students to realise the importance of learning and perfecting the details of anterior teeth morphology and its effect on the appearance of a smile. Failure to relate anterior tooth morphology to aesthetics which is essentially one of their main functions represents a huge gap in dental anatomy teaching that we wanted to avoid in the updated module by introducing this exercise. 5 | CONCLUSION The updated module which involved clinically relevant lectures, dig - ital-based educational tools/ computer-assisted learning and a focus on dental aesthetics as an integral part of anterior tooth morphology learning was highly appreciated and rated by students. An update to the educational method of teaching dental anatomy and morphology is proposed, clinical dental anatomy teaching results in enhanced students’ engagement and assessment. More research and proper strategic planning for implementation of digital technology into the dental anatomy curriculum are needed to

chunks.content: teaching results in enhanced students’ engagement and assessment. More research and proper strategic planning for implementation of digital technology into the dental anatomy curriculum are needed to adequately utilise these resources. The biomechanical advantage of selective pressure impressions over mucocompressive techniques remains unclear. This study aimed to determine whether selective pressure techniques offer substantial biomechanical advantage over mucocompressive impressions using clinical computer simulation. MATERIALS AND METHODS. Two models were analyzed: Model C, with mucocompressive impression tray, and Model S, with selective pressure impression tray

ive impressions using clinical computer simulation. MATERIALS AND METHODS. Two models were analyzed: Model C, with mucocompressive impression tray, and Model S, with selective pressure impression tray with 10-mm diameter circular relief in the midline. Each model included the tray, polyvinyl siloxane (PVS), mucosa, cortical, and cancellous bone. Seven locations were designated, from which the results were analyzed. With a vertical load of 49 N on the palatal area, pressure, von Mises stress, and displacement were evaluated. Statistical analysis was performed using paired- samples t-test and effect size estimation (Cohen’s d). RESUL TS. Both models generated mucosal displacement and stress transmission to the underlying structures upon load application. In Location 3, where the relief was placed, Model S exhibited lower pressure, stress, and displacement than Model C, indicating localized force reduction. Conversely, other locations exhibited higher values in Model S than in Model C.

Conversely, other locations exhibited higher values in Model S than in Model C. Low stress in bone for both trays suggested that tray design had minimal effect on bone. All variations demonstrated small effect sizes (d ≤ 0.2), despite statistical significance (P < .007). CONCLUSION. Selective pressure trays modified tissue loading locally at the relief site; however, these did not seem to provide a substantial biomechanical advantage, particularly on bone. Their clinical relevance remains limited and needs further supporting evidence. ndicating its superiority over mucocompressive technique.5-7 Excessive pressure on the edentulous ridge has been linked to tissue ischemia, bone resorption, and pain, which may subsequently compromise denture fit and function. 8,9 Moreover, some studies propose that selective pressure impression technique more effectively distributes forces across the denture-bear- ing tissues, thereby, improving denture retention and stability while lowering localized stress concen- trations.10-12 If impression techniques can be further improved, this will, in turn, improve the quality and outcome of the dentures. Studies on pressure distribution patterns between selective and mucocompressive impressions, how- ever, show minimal differences when compared, which helps reduce concerns about the clinical need of including custom tray relief areas during impres - sion-making.5-7 Though the selective pressure impres- sion technique is still extensively taught and used, its clinical justification continues

The results between Model C and Model S revealed statistically significant differences in all locations in terms of pressure distribution, von Mises stress, and displacement values. Model S consis - tently exhibited higher values than Model C in six out of seven locations, specifically, Locations 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, and 7. In contrast, at Location 3, where the relief was present, the results in Model S revealed reduced pressure, von Mises stress, and displacement val- ues. Further supporting the results of this research is previous evi- dence showing that pressure distribution in impres - sion-making is influenced more by anatomical differ - ences than by the impression technique itself.47,48 The findings of this study inquire the clinical jus - tification for utilizing selective pressure methods as a more superior and effective impression technique than mucocompressive impressions. Should no notable benefit be observed, dental professionals may reevaluate their clinical procedures and proto - cols, and perhaps simplify impression methods with- out compromising treatment quality, especially in situations where time and material efficiency are of paramount concern. From a clinical standpoint, the findings of this study may indicate that, despite the selective pressure technique being based on a support-oriented meth- odology that directs functional load to stress-bearing areas while alleviating non-stress-bearing tissues, its biomechanical benefit appears to be limited. In this study, tray relief resulted in only localized decreases in pressure, stress, and displacement at the relief site. Nonetheless, relief should not be regarded as unnec - essary. In addition to being helpful for support, tray relief has practical benefits as it facilitates re-impres - sions when the surfaces are rough or distorted.

In addition to being helpful for support, tray relief has practical benefits as it facilitates re-impres - sions when the surfaces are rough or distorted. It may also help alleviate discomfort in areas that are sensi- tive or have undergone surgery. Thus, although the current results show that tray relief may have a min - imal effect on biomechanics, the clinical rationale for protecting fragile tissues and making procedures more efficient remains relevant. As a result, the deci- sion whether to provide relief or not may be more influenced by efficiency and individual anatomical considerations rather than by expectation of a signifi- cant biomechanical advantage. Dynamic tis - sue displacement resulting from the fluid behavior of the impression material during tray seating may not be captured in the current simulation. Furthermore, excluded from this study were changes in muco - sal thickness or patient-specific anatomical varia- tions, which might affect displacement and pressure and stress distribution, and in this study, the mucosa was modeled as a homogeneous and linearly elastic material. In reality, oral mucosa has non-linear and viscoelastic properties, which may affect the accu- racy of stress and pressure distribution in the simula- tion. Furthermore, the study does not include direct clinical observations or patient-based data, limiting the translation of findings to actual practice. More sophisticated computational methods, for example, Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) 49,50 model- ing, could offer more dynamic simulations of impres - sion pressure effects, thus providing deeper under - standing of how various impression techniques affect tissue adaptation over time. The integration of 3D-printed trays and AI-driven impression analysis, in line with the advancement of digital dentistry, has the potential to significantly enhance impression tech- niques for edentulous patients. CONCLUSION The results of this finite element analysis indicate that the selective pressure impression tray may have an influence in the mucosal pressure and displace - ment values. However, the von Mises stress appears to have a negligible effect on both cortical and can- cellous bone. Although the selective pressure impres- sion tray evidently reduced the pressure, stress, and displacement values, its clinical impact appears to be clinically negligible. Due to this, the selective pressure impression technique may not provide a clear bio - mechanical advantage, and hence, the clinical appli- cation of selective pressure impression technique should be further investigated. chunks.content: College, Muscat, Oman The formulation of core syllabuses for the biomedical sciences within medical and dental courses is partially driven by the need to cope with decreased time allocations for these subjects as a result of major curricular changes taking place worldwide. There is also a requirement to deal with the request for increased clinical relevance. In response to such demands, the International Federation of Associations of Anatomists (IFAA) is devising core syllabuses for the anatomical sciences relating to the education and training of both scientiﬁc and clinical professions. The process initially involves using Delphi Panels con- sisting of a team of anatomists, scientists, and clinicians who evaluate syllabus content in detail and accord each element/topic ‘essential,’ ‘important,’ ‘accept- able,’ or ‘not required’ status. Their conjectures, published on the IFAA website, provide merely a framework to enable other stakeholders to comment. The approach is international in

The approach is international in scope, is conceptually ‘democratic,’ and is develop- mentally ﬂuid in being readily available for amendment. The aim is to set inter- nationally recognized standards and thus to provide guidelines concerning anatomical knowledge when engaged in course development. This article presents the deliberations of an IFAA Delphi Panel into a core syllabus for oral anatomy, histology, and embryology within the dental curriculum. Clin. Anat. 31:231–249, 2018. chunks.content: have often led to a reduction in the time available for the teaching of basic sciences, especially it seems for the anatomical sciences (Drake et al., 2002, 2009, 2014). It has been argued that these reductions have unfortunate consequences for the learning and teach- ing experiences of students, for the professional esteem in which a healthcare profession is held by laypersons, and also for patient safety (e.g., Goodwin, 2000, Kahan et al., 2001; Kidder , 2002; Ellis, 2002; Lynn-Macrae et al., 2004; Moxham et al., 2016). In response to the changes, some educators have rea- soned that there should be a greater focus on a core curriculum of the most clinically-relevant topics within the anatomical sciences (e.g., Heylings, 2002; Older , 2004; Craig et al., 2010). There are two main reasons for developing core syllabuses. First, as a response to the decline in con- tent of anatomy in healthcare courses by laying out what educators consider to be a syllabus that permits the teaching of a

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: for developing core syllabuses. First, as a response to the decline in con- tent of anatomy in healthcare courses by laying out what educators consider to be a syllabus that permits the teaching of a discipline in a coherent manner . Sec- ond, to counter the lack of sufﬁciently detailed guide- lines/outcomes from professional bodies beyond the broadest of statements that often do little more than afﬁrm that basic sciences should be taught (e.g., GMC, 1993, 2009; GDC, 2012). Orsbon et al. (2014), while exploring whether there is a ‘core’ of anatomical knowledge that is essential for clinical practice in medicine as some educators have suggested (Louw et al., 2009; Abu-Hijleh et al., 2010; Chapuis et al., 2010), have concluded that it is possible to formulate a guide to that knowledge which is generally accepted by anatomists and all those who use anatomical knowledge professionally, while not abandoning the critical evaluation that makes anatomy a scientiﬁc dis- cipline. This has been

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: h is generally accepted by anatomists and all those who use anatomical knowledge professionally, while not abandoning the critical evaluation that makes anatomy a scientiﬁc dis- cipline. This has been described by Young (2007) as devising a balance between universal knowledge and discipline critical evaluation. A further reason for developing core syllabuses is to provide a guide for students to navigate through the extraordinary multi- plicity of sources of information relating to the ana- tomical sciences. There have been several attempts to design core syllabuses for gross anatomy in the UK, US, and Europe, all of them focusing on medical anatomy and each varying in their approach, style, and scope (Leonard et al., 1996; Grifﬁoen et al., 1999; McHan- well et al., 2007; Orsbon et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2016a,b). Those produced by the American Associa- tion of Clinical Anatomists (Leonard et al., 1996) and the Dutch Anatomical Society (Grifﬁoen et al., 1999) were both very

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2016a,b). Those produced by the American Associa- tion of Clinical Anatomists (Leonard et al., 1996) and the Dutch Anatomical Society (Grifﬁoen et al., 1999) were both very detailed, whereas the syllabus pro- duced by the Anatomical Society in the UK and Ireland (McHanwell et al., 2007), and subsequently revised using a Delphi process (Smith et al., 2016a,b), was formulated as a set of learning outcomes intended as a ‘common sense’ approach that stands between the very broad statements set out by the General Medical Council (GMC) in Tomorrow’s Doctors (GMC, 2015) and the more highly prescriptive and detailed approaches. These two different approaches have clear advantages and disadvantages. The main advan- tage of a ‘non-detailed syllabus’ is its perceived ﬂexi- bility , being able to accommodate local variations in content as well as differences in expertise of the staff teaching the course. The advantage of the more ‘detailed syllabus’ is to avoid

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: ved ﬂexi- bility , being able to accommodate local variations in content as well as differences in expertise of the staff teaching the course. The advantage of the more ‘detailed syllabus’ is to avoid syllabuses being so ﬂexi- ble that they lead to unacceptable variation between courses. In contrast to gross anatomy, published core sylla- buses for specialist anatomical sciences are scarce. Core syllabuses for the anatomical sciences in the medical course, under the auspices of the Interna- tional Federation of Associations of Anatomists (IFAA), have been published for head and neck anatomy (T ubbs et al., 2014; T ubbs and Paulk, 2015), for neu- roanatomy (Moxham et al., 2015) and for embryology and teratology (Fakoya et al., 2017). In addition, Leonard et al. (2000) have presented a core syllabus for embryology (but not teratology) in the medical curriculum. For dentistry , core syllabuses for the ana- tomical sciences have yet to be formulated, although the Association for Dental

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: ore syllabus for embryology (but not teratology) in the medical curriculum. For dentistry , core syllabuses for the ana- tomical sciences have yet to be formulated, although the Association for Dental Education in Europe (ADEE) have provided some suggestions for a core biomedical science curriculum. Within this document are some guidelines for the teaching of oral anatomy , histology, and embryology (T able 1). However , the approach is ‘broad-brush’ and has not involved a Delphi Panel that has membership beyond Europe. This article describes the results of the deliberations of an international Del- phi Panel, set up by the IFAA, that analyses in detail items or topics for oral anatomy , histology , and embryology that could be taught within the dental course. From this, a core syllabus can be constructed that, in addition to listing essential/core topics, recog- nizes other topics that can be recommended and yet others that need not be taught. TABLE 1. chunks.content: METHODS The approach adopted by the IFAA in formulating core syllabuses in the anatomical sciences, including a thorough discussion of the guiding principles, has already been published by Moxham et al. (2014). The process is divided into three stages. The initial stage requires the creation of a Delphi Panel that consists of approximately 20 persons from different countries who have expertise in the subject area. The Delphi Panel for oral anatomy , histology , and embryology consisted of four members from the UK; two from the USA; two from Portugal; two from Scandinavia; two from Australia and New Zealand; one from France; one from Oman; one from Italy; one from Greece; one from South Africa; one from Russia. The age ranged from 31 to 70 1 years. Over 90% of the panelists were engaged in oral biology research. Seventy-eight percent have a dental clinical qualiﬁcation. Fourteen were writers of textbooks of oral anatomy. All of the panelists were teachers of dental students and 90%

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: d in oral biology research. Seventy-eight percent have a dental clinical qualiﬁcation. Fourteen were writers of textbooks of oral anatomy. All of the panelists were teachers of dental students and 90% reported that they had major involvements in teaching dental students. The coordinator was Professor Bernard Moxham from the UK. The high esteem of the panel is indicated by the panelists having published nearly 1,500 research papers in peer-refereed journals and having written nearly 80 textbooks/research monographs on various topics relating to oral biology. This Delphi Panel was provided with a detailed list of topics so as to avoid a ‘broad brush’ approach to the task. The topic list was obtained by analysis of three contemporary oral anatomy textbooks (namely , Nanci, 2012; Atkinson and Jowett, 2015; Berkovitz et al., 2017). Subsequently , each panel member eval- uated each item or topic in the list according to whether it should be considered ‘essential, ’ ‘impor- tant, ’

Subsequently , each panel member eval- uated each item or topic in the list according to whether it should be considered ‘essential, ’ ‘impor- tant, ’ ‘acceptable, ’ or ‘not required’ in a core syllabus. A blank section was also made available for comments from the panel members, although few signiﬁcant comments were received. The topic list in the survey questionnaire comprised 258 items or topics in oral anatomy , histology , and embryology (three items relating to the general appearance of the mouth, 10 topics related to dento-osseous structures, 17 items for the regional topography of the mouth and related areas such as the TMJ, six learning outcomes relating to the vasculature and innervation of the mouth, six items concerning sectional anatomy , 12 topics for functional anatomy, 21 items for enamel and amelo- genesis, four learning outcomes for investing organic layers on enamel surfaces, 23 items for dentine and dentinogenesis,

chunks.content: nal anatomy , 12 topics for functional anatomy, 21 items for enamel and amelo- genesis, four learning outcomes for investing organic layers on enamel surfaces, 23 items for dentine and dentinogenesis, eight learning outcomes for cemen- tum, 24 items for the periodontal ligament, tooth sup- port and root and periodontium development, 11 items for alveolar bone, 17 topics related to the oral mucosa, 21 items for the development of the face and palate, seven learning outcomes for the development of the jaws, six items for the development of the tongue and salivary glands, 23 items relating to early tooth development, tooth eruption and the develop- ment of the dentitions, three learning outcomes relat- ing to dental ageing, and 36 topics relating to comparative dental anatomy). The questionnaire included 62 items that had signiﬁcant and direct clini- cal applications (i.e., approximately 25% of the total items). Based upon the decisions of the panellists, each item was now categorized according to the following general rule discussed by Moxham et al. (2014). Where 60% of the panellists considered an item as being essential, this was categorized as being ‘core (essential). ’ Where between 30% and 59% of the panellists classiﬁed an item as being essential, the topic was designated as being ‘recommended. ’ Classi- ﬁcation of ‘acceptable’ or ‘not required’ came when the panellists only recorded essential designations between 20% and 29% and <20%, respectively. Although it was established that borderline judgments would be decided by looking at categories other than ‘essential, ’ because of the consensus among the pan- ellists this was found to be unnecessary . This is the stage at which the ﬁndings of the Delphi Panel are now presented to a more wide-ranging audi- ence through this article (and eventually through the IFAA website: http://www.ifaa.net/committees/ana- tomical-education-ﬁpae/ﬁpae-core-syllabuses-project/). Stages 2 and 3 of the development of the core oral anat- omy, histology, and embryology syllabus do not involve the Delphi Panel but are based upon the comments, and suggested amendments, from anatomical and dental societies, individual dental academics, oral biologists and anatomists, and dental clinicians on a global basis. The results of these deliberations will be reviewed and modiﬁed on a regular and continuous basis by the IFAA’s Federative International Programme for Anatomical Education. chunks.content: describing the Delphi process to be used by the IFAA, we await the responses of stakeholders other than the Delphi panelists to further develop the core syllabus. It is instructive to compare the core syllabus from the ADEE (see T able 1) with the IFAA syllabus reported here. The ADEE syllabus differs in several important respects from the topic list which is presented here derived from a Delphi process. First, and most obvi- ously, the ADEE syllabus is formulated very simply and has the advantage of being brief. The IFAA syllabus, on the other hand, is signiﬁcantly more detailed and ﬁne- grained in its approach. In this regard, it is of consider- ably more value to curriculum planners than the rather broad outcomes set out in the ADEE syllabus. T o elabo- rate, one can envisage a situation where one dental school provides its students with just a bare outline of the “composition, structure/function relationships” of the periodontal ligament while a different school pro- vides an

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: tuation where one dental school provides its students with just a bare outline of the “composition, structure/function relationships” of the periodontal ligament while a different school pro- vides an extensive account of the tissue. In both instan- ces, their curricula would satisfy the ADEE syllabus as it presently stands. Given that the topic list for the IFAA syllabus has been derived using a research process conducted with experts, we would argue that it has more validity . However , there is another key difference. The ADEE document intends learning to be much more directed to clinical relevance and is therefore more utilitarian and instrumentalist (for arguments against utilitarian/instrumentalist approaches in healthcare courses see Moxham and Pias, 2017). While we would agree that, in a professional programme such as den- tistry , the clinical dimension cannot be overlooked (indeed 25% of the items in the IFAA syllabus relate directly to the dental clinic), we are also of the

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: t, in a professional programme such as den- tistry , the clinical dimension cannot be overlooked (indeed 25% of the items in the IFAA syllabus relate directly to the dental clinic), we are also of the view that it is critical for clinical learning to take place in meaning- ful contexts where there is an adequate foundation of basic science taught early on in a dental programme that can then be built upon as clinical experience devel- ops in students at later stages of their course. The dan- ger , as we see it, of too early an exposure to clinical content is that this could potentially compromise learn- ing of basic science. It is recognized that ‘time on task’ is crucial for effective learning; the more time spent on learning a topic the more likely effective learning is going to occur . This has been recognized speciﬁcally in relation to anatomy (Bergman et al., 2008) but also to learning more generally (Gibbs, 2010). We would also suggest that, not only could learning of basic

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: cur . This has been recognized speciﬁcally in relation to anatomy (Bergman et al., 2008) but also to learning more generally (Gibbs, 2010). We would also suggest that, not only could learning of basic sciences be compromised if courses are over-loaded with clinical content early on, but also that one runs the risk of depriving students of disciplinary knowledge that is of critical importance in developing students’ predictive capacities and the ability to construct new knowledge. Young (2007) and Land (2016) have both stressed the importance of disciplinary knowledge (termed ‘power- ful knowledge’ by Young) in this process. Indeed, for the aims set out by the ADEE they emphasize the need to: “reinforce the importance of the biomedical scien- ces as key elements of the curriculum which underpin all areas of dental practice” (ADEE, 2016). The approach being advocated in the IFAA syllabus reported here is one of laying a foundation of basic science early on in a programme and then

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: ich underpin all areas of dental practice” (ADEE, 2016). The approach being advocated in the IFAA syllabus reported here is one of laying a foundation of basic science early on in a programme and then employing the methodol- ogy of a spiral curriculum in which concepts are pro- gressively elaborated and set in more realistic clinical contexts as clinical experience develops [i.e., as advo- cated by Brunner; see Olson (2007)]. All topics listed within the ADEE syllabus are cov- ered in the IFAA syllabus and are regarded as core. In only one respect is a topic listed in the ADEE syllabus that is not included in the IFAA syllabus, namely: “an appreciation of the relevance of an understanding of crown and root morphology to restorative dentistry , endodontics and oral surgery.” This omission in the IFAA syllabus again relates to the debate concerning the extent to which oral anatomy, histology , and embryology should primarily have an instrumentalist or utilitarian basis that has value

That said, it should be noted that no other clinical contexts are included within the present ADEE syllabus. This is a further area in which elements of the IFAA syllabus diverge from that of the ADEE syllabus. The advantages of core syllabuses are most keenly felt in situations where course guidelines are very widely drawn. Thus, while in the USA curriculum design needs to comply with nationwide LCME stand- ards in order for medical schools to receive accredita- tion, such nationwide, detailed, proscriptive standards are largely absent in the UK, Europe, and in other parts of the world. In general, what guidelines do exist are too widely drawn, be it from the General Dental Council (GDC) in the UK or from Bologna processes throughout Europe. Therefore, core syllabuses have the valuable function of making explicit, and readily available, tacit knowledge held by

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: ral Dental Council (GDC) in the UK or from Bologna processes throughout Europe. Therefore, core syllabuses have the valuable function of making explicit, and readily available, tacit knowledge held by professional anato- mists. T wo major related criticisms of the existing core syllabuses in anatomy have been raised. The ﬁrst is that they often amount to little more than a case of special pleading by professional groups or academics with vested interests. The second is that they are sel- dom arrived at by a rigorous process of consultation. A frequent way in which syllabuses of this kind are arrived at is through an organization assembling a committee of experts who, after more or less exten- sive consultation and deliberation among themselves, publish their results that are thus handed down “as tablets of stone.” These criticisms, which are not con- ﬁned to anatomy but apply to many such syllabuses from whatever source, often mean that core sylla- buses are ignored and consequently

chunks.book_title: Clinical Anatomy - 2017 - Moxham - The development of a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy  histology  and
chunks.content: down “as tablets of stone.” These criticisms, which are not con- ﬁned to anatomy but apply to many such syllabuses from whatever source, often mean that core sylla- buses are ignored and consequently have little impact. There are other possible reasons why these syllabuses have not been inﬂuential in shaping the curriculum. The ﬁrst is that they do not take account of how they will balance with other elements of the curriculum. The second is that over time there may be changes in the composition of the student body , changes in edu- cational technology or changes in the expectations of course designers about the ways by which students are expected to learn (e.g., a switch from didactic teaching to active and student-centered learning). The authors of core syllabus should be careful to emphasize that their approach must be independent of the method used for curriculum delivery . It is there- fore of great importance to recognize what a core syl- labus should not do. It does not

chunks.content: l to emphasize that their approach must be independent of the method used for curriculum delivery . It is there- fore of great importance to recognize what a core syl- labus should not do. It does not dictate where in a curriculum the topics should be taught nor does it imply that there are speciﬁc modes of delivery of the material (e.g., problem-based, scenario-based or more traditional didactic teaching). In conclusion, through a Delphi process, a core syllabus for the teaching of oral anatomy, histology, and embryology to dental students is presented here. Explaining how to assess the validity of the various current aspects of clinical decision making for the treatment of Class-II malocclusions in children and adolescents is inconsistent with the limited scope of an article. We will limit our talk to four questions for which the EBO helps to provide answers when making an informed choice of a thera - peutic option for our patients. Can two-phase treatment increase the amount of mandibular growth in the long run? Since 1879, and the birth of func - tional treatments with Kingsley, which introduced the expression “ Jumping the bite ” and recommended treating mandibular retrognathism with forced mandibular propulsion, countless types of functional devices, and therapeutic modalities have been proposed. Al -

Al - though many publications 18,43,69 have reported mandibular extension higher than those of untreated subjects after a functional treatment phase without the respective contributions, the treat- ment has been applied and favorable growth has been clearly established. On the other hand, long-term studies on the treatment of Class-II malocclu - sions showed that if mandibular growth could be greater than that of untreated subjects during the functional treat - ment phase, it then declined. chunks.content: J Dentofacial Anom Orthod 2017;20:206 13 PARADIGM ShIFT In ThE TREATMEnT OF CLASS-II MALOCCLUSIOnS In ChILDREn AnD ADOLESCEnTS The paradigm shift in clinical decision making, when taking into account the results of the best published data, has as a practical consequence, a paradigm shift in the treatment of Class-II maloc- clusions in children and teenagers. Abandonment of treatment of mandibular retrognathism by functional device Most patients with Class-II malocclu- sions exhibit mandibular retrognathism, rather than maxillary prognathism44,47. It seems medically relevant to target our therapeutic action on the precise cause of the dysmorphisms, and there- fore to favor the reduction of the man- dibular retrognathism. If the correction of a molar Class-II malocclusion and an incisor overhang does not pose any particular difficulties 46 (Case no. 1 of Fig. 3-9), the correction of a man - dibular retrognathism appears to be a more ambitious objective. Can it be achieved, with what

chunks.content: overhang does not pose any particular difficulties 46 (Case no. 1 of Fig. 3-9), the correction of a man - dibular retrognathism appears to be a more ambitious objective. Can it be achieved, with what device and thera - peutic sequence? These questions are at the heart of a controversy that still exists in our profession. The debate started in 1879, which saw the birth of functional treatments with Kingsley. At the beginning of the last century, Pierre Robin 59 advocated clearing the vital crossroads by wear - ing a monobloc. This device achieves a transverse expansion of the arches and maintains the mandible and tongue in an advanced position. Its indication is the treatment of glossoptosis, a con - dition where mandibular retrognathism is just one of the symptoms. Orthodontic treat - ment cannot alter skeletal disharmony persists, without improving or wors - ening. Orthodontic treatments correct Class-II malocclusions only using den - toalveolar compensation, and have no skeletal effects. Although American or- thodontists refute the role of functions on facial growth, European practition - ers continue to use functional thera - peutics. The publication of the results of stud- ies, on rats and macaques, by Pétro - vic54,64 and Mcnamara 31,45 has revived the debate. They showed the possibil - ity of an increase in mandibular length in these animals. however, did these data offer any hope that treatment for mandibular retrognathism would be effective? Would it be possible to treat a skeletal Class-II malocclusion with a long-term increase in mandibular length, similar to that of orthognathic surgery? The enthusiasm raised

chunks.content: athism would be effective? Would it be possible to treat a skeletal Class-II malocclusion with a long-term increase in mandibular length, similar to that of orthognathic surgery? The enthusiasm raised by the publication of these studies was tempered by the level of evidence of studies in animals, classified as being on the lowest level of the pyramid hierarchy of facts 27 ,50,60 (Fig. 26), and by the difficulty of a pos - sible transposition of the experimental conditions in humans. It seems difficult to propose the permanent wearing of a hyperpropulsor for the whole duration of the patient’s growth, such as with rats and monkeys, on which the stud - ies were conducted. nevertheless, the thought was still firmly anchored that only a first phase of treatment by functional device al - lowed the orthopedic correction of a Class-II malocclusion, by modifying the direction and amount of mandibular growth. chunks.content: J Dentofacial Anom Orthod 2017;20:206 17 PARADIGM ShIFT In ThE TREATMEnT OF CLASS-II MALOCCLUSIOnS In ChILDREn AnD ADOLESCEnTS The end of the debate? It must be noted that the enthusias - tic hypothesis of an effective cure for mandibular retrognathism has given way to a false hope, which has been in- validated, publication after publication, by factual data. Why have we not closed this de - bate? Why have we not yet completely changed the treatment paradigm? Why are we still talking about a treatment for mandibular retrognathism, and not, simply, a correction of a Class-II maloc- clusion? Some of the explanations can be found in simple facts: – One is the persistence of the erro - neous belief that multiattachment devices, unlike functional devices, can only treat a Class-II malocclusion with dentoalveolar compensation, and possibly by maxillary retraction when the treatment is coupled with the use of an extraoral force; – Another is the apparent stability of Class-II malocclusions,

chunks.book_title: Paradigm Shift in the treatment of Class-II
chunks.content: n with dentoalveolar compensation, and possibly by maxillary retraction when the treatment is coupled with the use of an extraoral force; – Another is the apparent stability of Class-II malocclusions, which, if un- treated, do not appear to be mitigat- ed by growth 19,38. This widespread clinical observation casts doubt on the clinicians’ mistaken belief that mandibular growth may make a fa - vorable contribution to Class-II cor - rection. – These facts do not in any way chal - lenge the published data and the aforementioned conclusion of the debate. They are simply explained by the phenomenon of dentoalveo - lar compensation42,63. The dentoalveolar compensation phenomenon Björk and Skieller have shown that, for most patients, mandibular growth is greater than maxillary growth 10. In a Class-II patient, in the absence of treatment, occlusal meshing and labial-lingual interposition, prevent the excess of mandibular growth from participating in the correction of the Class-II occlusion8. Keywords: continuning professional development | peri- implant mucositis | peri- implantitis | periodontitis | vocational education and training ABSTRACT Aim: To (i) evaluate structured postgraduate part- time programs in periodontology, including those addressing peri- implant diseases, among members of the European Federation of Periodontology (EFP), (ii) the impact of the 2018 classification scheme and EFP clinical practice guidelines and (iii) propose a framework for periodontal vocational education and

chunks.content: ropean Federation of Periodontology (EFP), (ii) the impact of the 2018 classification scheme and EFP clinical practice guidelines and (iii) propose a framework for periodontal vocational education and training. Materials and Methods: A summary of relevant European guidelines for vocational education and training was compiled. In a survey and in a systematic review, current part- time programs in continuing professional education in periodontology as well as in prevention and management of peri- implant diseases were examined. The implementation and dissemination of the 2018 classification scheme and the EFP clinical practice guidelines were assessed by literature analysis. Based on these findings, a framework for periodontal vocational education and training was generated. chunks.content: 92 Journal of Clinical Periodontology, 2024 Results: Part- time programs for professional development in periodontology are established in nine EFP member countries. The systematic review identified lack of knowledge in prevention and management of peri- implant diseases among dental practition- ers and hygienists. Continuing professional development was found to be important for education in prevention, classification and management of periodontal as well as peri- implant diseases. The proposed European framework consists of an escalator model with three levels (certificate, diploma and master). Discussion: Considering the identified variation in the national programs, there is a need to improve education in periodontal and peri- implant diseases. The proposed framework will help harmonize the national structures. Conclusion: The proposed framework for part- time professional development is expected to enhance professional qualification. 1 | Introduction Periodontitis is the most common non- communicable disease in humans, leading to tooth loss and independently associated with premature mortality (Winning et al. 2021). Oral diseases (mostly periodontitis) are globally responsible for more years lost to disability than any other human disease (James et al. 2018 ). In addition to periodontology and the well- known traditional restorative concepts, implant dentistry has grown exponentially over the last decades and has become a standard of care in oral rehabilitation. While the initial provision of implant dentistry was limited to specialized professionals, today, straightforward implant procedures are increasingly performed by general dental practitioners (GDPs) (M. Sanz and Saphira 2009). Peri- implant diseases, especially peri- implantitis, represent a grow -

chunks.book_title: J Clinic Periodontology - 2024 - Meyle - Continuing Professional Development  CPD  and Vocational Education and Training
chunks.content: traightforward implant procedures are increasingly performed by general dental practitioners (GDPs) (M. Sanz and Saphira 2009). Peri- implant diseases, especially peri- implantitis, represent a grow - ing public health problem due to their high prevalence and their consequences (implant and implant- supported prosthesis loss), including substantial dental care costs (Herrera et al. 2023). Hence, the prevention and management of peri- implant dis - eases and conditions is of utmost importance and must be ad - equately addressed at the different levels of dental education. Still, in Europe, there is a paucity of dentists and dental profes - sionals with sufficient additional training in periodontology and implant dentistry for the treatment of more advanced cases of the diseases (Griffiths and Preshaw 2014 ). As early as in 1996, the European Federation for Periodontology (EFP) developed guidelines for postgraduate qualification, rec - ognizing that a specialization in periodontology

As early as in 1996, the European Federation for Periodontology (EFP) developed guidelines for postgraduate qualification, rec - ognizing that a specialization in periodontology and implant therapy is a prerequisite for improving the quality of care in these important fields in dentistry in European countries (EFP 2019 ). Already in conjunction with the Bologna Process in 2008, a need for further specialization was discussed (M. Sanz, Widstrom, and Eaton 2008). Then the 1st European Consensus Workshop on Periodontal Education, in 2009, strongly called for a pathway for a specialization at the European level, not only in orthodon - tics and oral surgery but also in periodontology (M. Sanz and Meyle 2010; Van der Velden and Sanz 2010). Since this consensus workshop (M. Sanz and Meyle 2010), four important developments within the field of periodontology and implant dentistry have been published within the last 5 years: 1. The 2018 Classification of Periodontal and

The 2018 Classification of Periodontal and Peri- Implant Diseases and Conditions (Caton et al. 2018). 2. Treatment of stage I–III periodontitis—The European Federation of Periodontology (EFP) S3 level clinical practice (M. Sanz et al. 2020 ). 3. Treatment of stage IV periodontitis: The EFP S3 level clini - cal practice guideline (Herrera et al. 2022 ). 4. Prevention and treatment of peri- implant diseases: The EFP S3 level clinical practice guideline (Herrera et al. 2023 ). These four bodies of work are inextricably linked. As part of the range of reclassified conditions affecting the periodontium, the 2017 World Workshop presented a new approach to the classifica- tion of periodontitis incorporating the concept of staging and grad- ing of disease (Tonetti, Greenwell, and Kornman 2018). The aim of this was to link disease

The aim of this was to link disease classification with approaches to pre - vention and treatment, as it describes not only disease severity and extent but also the degree of complexity and an individual's risk. Owing to the differences in the regulation of the educational systems in European countries, the establishment and accred - itation of a postgraduate education in periodontology based on EFP guidelines was found to be challenging, especially when fo- cusing on the ‘protected’ entity of a national specialist. Currently periodontology is a recognized specialty in 17 European coun - tries (Eaton et al. 2022). Since then, several consensus workshops from different orga - nizations have defined diverse educational pathways to obtain competences related to not only periodontology but also implant dentistry (Donos,

Throughout Europe, numerous programs have been imple - mented that provide knowledge transfer in the form of certif - icate, diploma and/or master's programs. The fourth level is related to the specialty programs that, in general, prepare spe - cialists to carry out complex surgical and/or restorative treat - ments (Donos, Mardas, and Buser 2009; Mattheos et al. 2009, 2010a). This last level of postgraduate training will not be ad - dressed in the present article. VET pro - grams today are increasingly structured into smaller modules or units, and there is evidence that several countries have introduced more flexible approaches that allow learners to accumulate smaller parts of qualifications that are assessed separately (Cedefop 2023a). Therefore, a more differentiated view might be more appropriate to optimize treatment options for our patients, taking into account that not all patients with periodontitis will require the services of a fully qualified spe - cialist but might be well served by a dentist with an additional qualification below that level. Importantly, these concepts are designed to complement the highest qualification level of specialist, rather than to offer an alternative, in view of the significant requirements for skilled healthcare practitioners. 2 | VET in Periodontology in Europe 2.1 | Aim of Review The objective of this review was to provide an overview over the

chunks.content: , in view of the significant requirements for skilled healthcare practitioners. 2 | VET in Periodontology in Europe 2.1 | Aim of Review The objective of this review was to provide an overview over the European regulations and recommendations for life- long learning and upskilling, and to get a more detailed picture based on a survey which was sent to all national societies, which are members of the EFP. As a consequence, recommen - dations are given for possible VET programs in periodontology after graduation. 2.2 | Methods Based on the European regulations and recommendations provided by different institutions of the European Union (EU), a short overview over professional qualification and VET is provided. For this purpose, the publications and recommendations of the EU and its affiliated institutions available on the websites of the EU, that is, the European Qualifications Network (Europass) and the European Center for the Development of Vocational Training (CEDEFOP), served as the

chunks.content: ed institutions available on the websites of the EU, that is, the European Qualifications Network (Europass) and the European Center for the Development of Vocational Training (CEDEFOP), served as the sources of information (Cedefop 2023b ; Europass 2008 ). In addition, the current situation in periodontology in the differ- ent European countries was investigated by a survey in the form of an Excel- based questionnaire. This was distributed by mail via the secretary of the EFP to the EFP delegates of all member coun- tries plus Armenia, Georgia and Morocco and to the International Associate members: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Lebanon, Mexico, Singapore, Taiwan and Uruguay. They were asked to contribute within a given time. Two gentle reminders were sent and the information received until September was gathered in one file. The respondents were contacted personally, in case of missing information. Based on the European VET initiative, the outcomes from the survey and in

Based on the European VET initiative, the outcomes from the survey and in consideration of the recommendations pro - vided by the first European workshop on education, organized by the EFP, a proposal for a VET program in periodontology is proposed (M. Sanz and Meyle 2010; Van der Velden and Sanz 2010). 2.3 | Results 2.3.1 | Regulatory Background in Europe Education is regulated in the EU through various routes or ‘processes’, usually named after the European city where the agreement was reached. Regulation of education is not a core competence of the EU; that is, educational processes are not directly regulated by Brussels, but rather influenced by the development of common principles and tools that are also generally applicable to non- EU countries. In dentistry, a life- long learning process is becoming increasingly important, as medical knowledge doubles

chunks.book_title: J Clinic Periodontology - 2024 - Meyle - Continuing Professional Development  CPD  and Vocational Education and Training
chunks.content: ent of common principles and tools that are also generally applicable to non- EU countries. In dentistry, a life- long learning process is becoming increasingly important, as medical knowledge doubles approximately every 72 days (Densen 2011). This review focuses on structured postgraduate education for already qualified practising dentists after ending their formal training. These educational measures, often (inap - propriately) summarized as continuing professional devel - opment (CPD) courses, are no longer ‘primary’ educational programs leading to a first qualification but intend to flexibly up- skill and/or re- skill the existing workforce to meet new challenges and opportunities. They fall under the umbrella of ‘Vocational Education and Training’ (VET), loosely gov - erned by the Bruges- Copenhagen Process, initiated by the EU institutions with the Declaration of Copenhagen in 2002 and further developed in the Communiqués of Maastricht (2004), Helsinki (2006), Bordeaux (2008)

chunks.book_title: J Clinic Periodontology - 2024 - Meyle - Continuing Professional Development  CPD  and Vocational Education and Training
chunks.content: Bruges- Copenhagen Process, initiated by the EU institutions with the Declaration of Copenhagen in 2002 and further developed in the Communiqués of Maastricht (2004), Helsinki (2006), Bordeaux (2008) and Bruges (2010), the Conclusions of Riga (2015) and the Osnabrück Declaration (2020) (Cedefop 1994 , 2010; 2020). The major governing principles of the Bruges- Copenhagen Process are the following: i. Life- long learning at any career stage, allowing for a step- wise, often flexible, part- time progress along the en - tire qualification range in the European Qualifications Framework (EQF) (Europass 2008 ); and ii. Linked to the above, to ensure mobility of learners by in - troducing a qualification and credit transfer scheme. chunks.content: 95 The EQF levels are compatible with the framework for qualifi - cations in the European higher education area (EHEA), created by the Bologna process (EHEA 2005; Ministers in charge for France 1998). In the EHEA, three cycles have been described corresponding to levels 6, 7 and 8 of the EQF: Cycle 1: Bachelor level, Cycle 2: Master level, Cycle 3: Doctoral level (EHEA 2005 ). 2.3.3 | European Credit System for Vocational Education and Training This system, the European Credit system for Vocational Education and Training (ECVET), is similar to the better known European Credit Transfer System (ECTS) that underpins the programs governed by the Bologna Process (EHEA 2015), but focuses on professionally applicable learning outcomes, rather than simply assessing academic workload (Cedefop 2009 ). ECVET tools and methodology comprise the description of qual- ifications in terms of units of learning outcomes with associated points, a transfer and accumulation process and complementary

chunks.book_title: J Clinic Periodontology - 2024 - Meyle - Continuing Professional Development  CPD  and Vocational Education and Training
chunks.content: op 2009 ). ECVET tools and methodology comprise the description of qual- ifications in terms of units of learning outcomes with associated points, a transfer and accumulation process and complementary documents such as learning agreements, transcripts of records and ECVET user guides. A unit is a component of a qualification, consisting of a coherent set of knowledge, skills and competence that can be assessed and validated with a number of associated ECVET points. In principle, a qualification consists of several units and is made up of the whole set of units. Thus, a learner can achieve a qualifi - cation by accumulating the required units, achieved in different countries and different contexts (formal and, where appropriate, non- formal and informal), in compliance with national leg - islation on accumulation of units and recognition of learning outcomes. A unit may be specific to a single qualification or common to several qualifications. The expected learning outcomes that define

chunks.book_title: J Clinic Periodontology - 2024 - Meyle - Continuing Professional Development  CPD  and Vocational Education and Training
chunks.content: islation on accumulation of units and recognition of learning outcomes. A unit may be specific to a single qualification or common to several qualifications. The expected learning outcomes that define a unit can be achieved regardless of where or how they are achieved. A unit is therefore not to be confused with a component of a formal program of study or training. There are some requirements for the composition and properties of a unit (Table S2.1). Procedures and guidelines for the assessment, validation, ac - cumulation and recognition of units of learning outcomes are developed by the relevant competent institutions and partners involved in the training process. Similar to the European ECTS, 60 ECVET credits are the equivalent to a full year of study or work in VET. 2.3.4 | Outcomes From the Survey: Types of VET in Periodontology—Current Situation in Some European Countries Part- time VET programs are currently accredited in Austria, France, Germany, Luxembourg, Spain and
