The above results indicated that the multifunctional nanoplatform offers a novel treatment for peri- implantitis by ex- hibiting both antibacterial and anti- inflammatory effects. 3.1.2 | Release of Ions In addition to generating ROS and photoactivated antimicro - bial strategies (PDT/PTT), metal- based NPs, particularly those composed of Ag, Cu, and Zn, exhibit potent antimicrobial ef - fects through sustained ion release [ 140]. These metal ions can cross bacterial cell membranes and interfere with essen - tial cellular processes such as DNA replication and repair, en - ergy production, and respiration [ 141]. The surfaces of relevant Gram- negative bacteria implicated in periodontitis and peri- implantitis, including P. gingivalis , F. nucleatum , T. denticola , and T. forsythia, are characterized by a negatively charged lipo - polysaccharide layer [ 142,

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: mplicated in periodontitis and peri- implantitis, including P. gingivalis , F. nucleatum , T. denticola , and T. forsythia, are characterized by a negatively charged lipo - polysaccharide layer [ 142, 143]. This anionic nature is believed to facilitate both the interactions with and the subsequent in - ternalization of metal ions through increasing the permeability of bacterial membranes. Following intracellular accumulation, metal ions induce cellular toxicity by interacting with cytoplas - mic content. For instance, free Ag ions possess a strong affinity for thiol groups (- SH), which can disrupt enzyme functionality and damage the disulfide bonds (S- S) essential for preserving protein structures [144]. Intracellular biomolecules like cysteine and GSH featuring - SH groups on their side chains play pivotal roles in cellular respiration, energy production, and antioxida - tion. This modification led to disruptions in the integrity of the bacterial membrane, subsequently promoting the generation of ROS. It was also observed that small, surface- functionalized NPs can directly disrupt intracellular structures and lead to cell death. For example, AgNPs were found to induce DNA condensation, thereby inhibiting DNA replication and consequently preventing cellular reproduction [148]. To achieve targeted antibacterial activity, innovative strategies are being explored, such as harnessing the bacterial recognition capabili - ties of macrophage membranes [149]. This approach allows NPs to selectively bind to specific bacteria, which is of significant in - terest in the development of precision and personalized therapy. In a pioneering study in this area, Wang et al. developed Au-

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: Ps to selectively bind to specific bacteria, which is of significant in - terest in the development of precision and personalized therapy. In a pioneering study in this area, Wang et al. developed Au- Ag nanocages coated with membranes from bacteria- pretreated macrophages [150]. These nanocages demonstrated target deliv- ery performance and enabled the on- demand release of antibac- terial drugs upon stimulation with NIR light. Notably, different NPs may possess multiple and distinct anti - bacterial mechanisms. Despite these advances, conventional agents such as H 2O2 remain widely used due to their broad- spectrum antimicrobial effects and well- established proteolytic properties [151]. These findings highlight the need to balance innovation with established clinical practices, suggesting that future strategies may benefit from combining the precision of nanomaterials with the proven effectiveness of traditional agents. Moreover, given the structural variability of bacteria at both

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: ing that future strategies may benefit from combining the precision of nanomaterials with the proven effectiveness of traditional agents. Moreover, given the structural variability of bacteria at both species and strain levels, continued exploration of these mechanisms for targeting periodontitis and peri- implantitis- associated pathogens is essential for optimizing therapeutic selectivity. 3.2 | Nanoparticles for Tissue Regeneration NPs have shown great promise in enhancing osteogenesis, an - giogenesis, and osseointegration in periodontal and implant therapies [152, 153]. By interacting with cells and modulating signaling pathways, NPs and/or the released ions promote vas - cularization and bone regeneration, addressing both soft and hard tissue defects while facilitating implant- host integration. The molecular mechanisms underlying NP- mediated tissue regeneration involve well- characterized signaling pathways regulating osteogenesis (e.g., BMP/Smad, FAK/RhoA/YAP, Wnt/β-

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: ant- host integration. The molecular mechanisms underlying NP- mediated tissue regeneration involve well- characterized signaling pathways regulating osteogenesis (e.g., BMP/Smad, FAK/RhoA/YAP, Wnt/β- catenin), osteoclast inhibition (e.g., RANK/RANKL, NF- κB), angiogenesis (e.g., VEGF, TGF- β, NOS), and tissue homeostasis (e.g., Notch, Hedgehog, YAP/TAZ), as reviewed elsewhere [154–156]. The specific NPs and their corresponding regenerative capabilities in enhancing periodontal and peri- implant tissue regeneration are discussed. Osteogenesis and osseointegration, the process of bone forma - tion, can be significantly improved by NPs. For instance, various NPs, including bioactive nanoceramics (e.g., nanohydroxyapa - tite (nHA), bioactive glass, and calcium phosphate), polymeric nanomaterials (e.g., chitosan, gelatin), and carbon- based NPs are often applied directly or incorporated into graft scaffolds or guided tissue regeneration (GTR) membranes. These NPs pro - mote bone

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: nanomaterials (e.g., chitosan, gelatin), and carbon- based NPs are often applied directly or incorporated into graft scaffolds or guided tissue regeneration (GTR) membranes. These NPs pro - mote bone regeneration by stimulating the differentiation of mesenchymal cells (MSCs) into osteoblasts, enhancing miner - alization, and providing space maintenance for bone ingrowth [154, 157]. In addition to osteogenesis, NPs can facilitate angio - genesis, which involves the formation of new blood vessels, a crucial process for nutrient supply, wound healing, and tissue regeneration [158]. Diverse NPs such as metal or metal oxide NPs (e.g., AuNPs, AgNPs, ZnO NPs, CeO 2 NPs), bioactive glass NPs, carbon- based, and graphene- based nanomaterials can in - fluence endothelial cell behavior, promote vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) se - cretion, and improve blood vessel formation [159]. Some nanomaterials also possess immunomodulatory effects that create

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: scular endothelial growth factors (VEGF) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) se - cretion, and improve blood vessel formation [159]. Some nanomaterials also possess immunomodulatory effects that create a favorable microenvironment for alleviating in- flammation and promoting tissue regeneration [160]. These NPs achieve this by either scavenging ROS or targeting immune cells [160–162]. For example, Mn nanozyme has been shown to generate oxygen by scavenging ROS, thereby further inhibiting anaerobic bacteria and promoting periodontal bone regenera- tion in a rat periodontitis model [163]. Modified formulations of CeO 2 NPs, loaded onto MSN and functionalized with PEG, have been found to effectively protect periodontal ligament stem cells and reduce alveolar bone loss in experimental periodontitis [164, 165]. 3.3 | Nanoparticles for Drug Delivery and Controlled Release NPs have garnered significant attention as drug delivery sys - tems due to their ability to enhance the bioavailability,

chunks.content: ntitis [164, 165]. 3.3 | Nanoparticles for Drug Delivery and Controlled Release NPs have garnered significant attention as drug delivery sys - tems due to their ability to enhance the bioavailability, stabil - ity, and controlled release of therapeutic agents. Drug- loaded NPs can be used to deliver antimicrobial agents, growth fac - tors, or anti- inflammatory drugs directly to infected or dam - aged tissues, promoting healing, tissue regeneration, and infection control with enhanced efficacy and minimal adverse effects. Moreover, NPs can protect drugs from the influence of pH and enzymatic degradation. For example, Alcalase 2.4 L FG, a serine endopeptidase protease, was loaded in CuS NPs to improve its stability. In addition to serving as a protease carrier, CuS NPs are also known as excellent photodynamic and photothermal agents. Under NIR light irradiation, this drug delivery system exerted dual therapeutic effects, effec - tively inhibiting F. nucleatum biofilms and reducing bone

Under NIR light irradiation, this drug delivery system exerted dual therapeutic effects, effec - tively inhibiting F. nucleatum biofilms and reducing bone re - sorption and inflammation in rat periodontitis models [ 166]. In another experimental periodontitis model, local adminis - tration of curcumin- loaded PLGA NPs effectively suppressed inflammation and bone resorption [ 26]. To improve regenera - tive potential, amorphous calcium phosphate NPs loaded with growth differentiation factor 5 (GDF5), a growth factor crucial for MSC differentiation and human periodontal ligament cells (hPDLCs) proliferation, demonstrated a controlled release over 30 days in vitro. Furthermore, GDF5- loaded amorphous calcium phosphate NPs successfully guided human periodon - tal ligament stem cells (hPDLSCs) toward bone differentiation in a rat maxillofacial burr hole bone defect model, showcasing their potential in regenerative therapies [ 27]. Subsequent plaque staining results further confirmed that DM is a powerful tool for removing plaque from the surface of TiO 2 implants (Figure 7D). chunks.content: ng peri- implantitis. 3.4 | Nanoparticles for Theranostic Application Dental plaque biofilms drive periodontitis and peri- implantitis through complex microbial communities that exhibit site- specific heterogeneity and dynamic changes during disease progression. Precise identification and quantification of pathogenic microorganisms are essential for accurate diag - nosis and targeted therapy [ 168]. Recently, lanthanide- doped down- converted NPs have been introduced to enable real- time bacterial visualization through NIR- IIb fluorescence [ 163]. When functionalized with bacteria- targeting peptides such as ubiquicidin (UBI 29–41 ), those NPs achieved specific bacterial localization via electrostatic interactions with phosphatidyl - glycerol on bacterial membranes. This approach successfully visualized infection sites in rat periodontitis models under NIR- II illumination, demonstrating translational potential for clinical diagnostics. A comprehensive review of theranostic NPs in

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: essfully visualized infection sites in rat periodontitis models under NIR- II illumination, demonstrating translational potential for clinical diagnostics. A comprehensive review of theranostic NPs in periodontal and peri- implant disease management is available elsewhere [ 169]. 3.5 | Biodistribution and Toxicity of Nanoparticles The biodistribution and toxicity of NPs are critical consider - ations for their safe and effective use in periodontal and dental implant therapy. One of the key factors influencing NPs' toxic - ity, distribution, and clearance is particle size [ 170]. For locally applied NPs in periodontal pockets or around dental implants, size can influence the tissue penetration depth, retention time, and potential systemic exposure, particularly through inflamed periodontal and peri- implant vasculature. NPs smaller than 10 nm, while typically cleared rapidly from the body through renal excretion following systemic absorption, may diffuse too rapidly from periodontal

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: tal and peri- implant vasculature. NPs smaller than 10 nm, while typically cleared rapidly from the body through renal excretion following systemic absorption, may diffuse too rapidly from periodontal and peri- implant tissues, limiting therapeutic duration. In contrast, larger NPs (> 10 nm) offer the advantage of prolonged local retention for sustained therapeutic effects but are more likely to accumu - late in tissues and are cleared primarily by the liver and the mononuclear phagocyte system [ 171]. For instance, quantum dots with a hydrodynamic diameter below 5.5 nm are effi - ciently eliminated via the urinary system, whereas particles larger than 15 nm are restricted from renal clearance and tend to persist in the body for longer durations [ 172]. In certain instances, particle morphology can influence or tailor the ef - fects of particle size on the biodistribution and toxicity of NPs, as NP geometry also influences the cellular internalization process [ 173], offering further

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: phology can influence or tailor the ef - fects of particle size on the biodistribution and toxicity of NPs, as NP geometry also influences the cellular internalization process [ 173], offering further consideration for NPs design in periodontal and peri- implant applications. The degradability of NPs is equally critical in determining their biocompatibility and long- term safety. Biodegradable polymeric NPs—such as those based on PLGA or chitosan—undergo gradual hydrolysis or enzymatic degradation into non- toxic by- products. This property enhances their safety while facilitating sustained drug release during the critical treatment window, making them particularly advantageous for controlling acute or chronic inflammation and promoting tissue regeneration. In contrast, inorganic NPs, including those made from silica, gold, or metal oxides, typically degrade more slowly. While this pro - longed stability can be beneficial for durable implant surface modifications that require long-

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: including those made from silica, gold, or metal oxides, typically degrade more slowly. While this pro - longed stability can be beneficial for durable implant surface modifications that require long- term antibacterial efficacy and osseointegration enhancement, it raises concerns regarding tissue accumulation and potential chronic toxicity. Therefore, engineering NPs with tailored degradation profiles is essential to maximize therapeutic outcomes while minimizing adverse effects. Despite these well- acknowledged design considerations, a crit - ical knowledge gap persists between extensive research on in - travenous NPs pharmacokinetics and the scarcity of data on NPs administered locally in periodontal pockets and around dental implants. These sites present unique challenges, such as dynamic fluid flow (e.g., gingival crevicular fluid (GCF)), me - chanical disruption (e.g., mastication, tongue movement), and inflamed, highly vascularized tissues that facilitate systemic absorption.

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: ynamic fluid flow (e.g., gingival crevicular fluid (GCF)), me - chanical disruption (e.g., mastication, tongue movement), and inflamed, highly vascularized tissues that facilitate systemic absorption. Because of these distinctive features, designing NPs that achieve optimal size and morphology to balance effective local retention with safe clearance remains poorly understood. Elucidating local retention kinetics, tissue penetration patterns through diseased periodontal tissues, and potential systemic ex - posure represents a critical research priority. Such knowledge will enable rational NPs formulation design tailored to peri - odontal environments, optimizing therapeutic outcomes while minimizing off- target effects in periodontology and implant dentistry. 4 | Clinical Studies of Nanoparticles in Periodontology NPs hold significant potential in periodontology, with possible applications spanning the diagnosis, prevention, and antimi - crobial treatment of periodontitis, as well as

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: particles in Periodontology NPs hold significant potential in periodontology, with possible applications spanning the diagnosis, prevention, and antimi - crobial treatment of periodontitis, as well as the regeneration of periodontal and soft tissues. While preclinical studies have established the mechanistic basis for these applications, clinical translation requires validation in human subjects. This section reviews evidence from clinical trials that assess NPs- assisted in- terventions in periodontal therapy, offering insights into their real- world effectiveness, safety, and practical implementation in clinical settings. 4.1 | Nanoparticles in the Diagnosis of Periodontitis One of the key challenges in contemporary periodontology is diagnosis, particularly the identification of individuals at risk 16000765, 0, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jre.70075 by Aix-Marseille Universitaet, Wiley Online Library on [29/06/2026]. chunks.content: 15 Journal of Periodontal Research, 2026 of future severe attachment loss, as well as the difficulty of applying diagnostic procedures at a population level. In this context, the use of biomarkers for periodontitis has emerged as one of the most actively researched areas of investigation [174–176]. Metal NPs, such as gold, silver, and copper oxide, have demon - strated good potential for diagnosis due to their favorable op - tical, catalytic, and biocompatible properties [ 177]. AuNPs are recognized for their stability and tunable surface functional - ization, which enable them to bind selectively to biomarkers [178, 179 ]. For example, AuNP- based biosensors have been used to detect gingipain activity—a key indicator of P. gingiva - lis presence [ 180]—with high sensitivity, achieving detection limits well below clinically relevant concentrations [ 181, 182]. In addition, novel voltammetric biosensors enhanced with AuNPs and specific antibodies have successfully detected and

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: ieving detection limits well below clinically relevant concentrations [ 181, 182]. In addition, novel voltammetric biosensors enhanced with AuNPs and specific antibodies have successfully detected and quantified matrix metalloproteinase- 8 (MMP- 8) in saliva col - lected from periodontitis patients, which serves as an essen - tial indicator of inflammation severity (Figure 8A) [184, 185]. Other metal NPs like AgNPs have also been integrated into bi - osensing platforms, where their unique plasmonic properties facilitate colorimetric detection. For instance, sensors based on the geometric modification of AgNPs) have been used to monitor possible periodontitis biomarkers such as alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and IL- 1β in human saliva, achieving remarkably low detection limits compared to traditional as - says (Figure 8B–D) [182]. In another approach, AgNPs were incorporated into a wearable biosensor for in situ periodon - titis monitoring through detecting salivary H 2S, which is as -

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: traditional as - says (Figure 8B–D) [182]. In another approach, AgNPs were incorporated into a wearable biosensor for in situ periodon - titis monitoring through detecting salivary H 2S, which is as - sociated with pathogenic anaerobic bacteria [ 186]. The sensor not only distinguished periodontitis patients, but also enabled the release of antibacterial drugs CHX, which was positively correlated with the concentration of Ag 2S, a product formed during the monitoring period. Similarly, biosensors employing hybrid nanostructures, such as gold nanobipyramids coated with silver nanoshells, leverage selective catalytic activities to generate distinct color changes corresponding to different biomarkers [ 187]. Copper oxide NPs (CuO NPs) have been utilized to construct non- enzymatic, highly electrocatalytic biosensors for detecting H 2O2 levels. By incorporating CuO NPs with materials such as chitosan and black phosphorus nanosheets, researchers have achieved sen - sors with low detection

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: lectrocatalytic biosensors for detecting H 2O2 levels. By incorporating CuO NPs with materials such as chitosan and black phosphorus nanosheets, researchers have achieved sen - sors with low detection limits and high sensitivity, capable of distinguishing between periodontitis patients and healthy indi - viduals (Figure 8E ) [183, 188]. In addition, magnetic NPs have been engineered into biosensing systems for rapid pathogen detection. For example, platforms that attach gingipain- specific peptides to magnetic nanobeads have demonstrated the ability to detect P. gingivalis at extremely low concentrations within 30 s [189]. The potential of such strat- egy was confirmed by examining saliva from periodontitis pa - tients and healthy controls. Portable diagnostic devices using magnetic NPs have also shown promise for point- of- care appli- cations by targeting key salivary biomarkers like neutrophil elas- tase and cathepsin- G, as validated by testing human saliva [190]. Fluorescent NPs,

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: ave also shown promise for point- of- care appli- cations by targeting key salivary biomarkers like neutrophil elas- tase and cathepsin- G, as validated by testing human saliva [190]. Fluorescent NPs, including up- converting NPs (UCNPs), offer another powerful diagnostic tool due to their high photostability and low background autofluorescence. UCNP- based platforms have been developed for both single and multiplex biomarker de- tection. A fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)- based nanoplatform employing SiO2- coated UCNPs was able to detect MMP- 2 activity in saliva obtained from patients with severe periodontitis [191], while a lateral flow immunoassay strip using green core–shell UCNPs facilitated the simultaneous detection of multiple biomarkers in clinical GCF and saliva samples, such as MMP- 8, IL- 1β, TNF- α, and microRNA- 21 with high sensitiv- ity and specificity [ 192, 193]. Additionally, organic fluorescent probes, such as a coumarin- based “turn- on” sensor,

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: va samples, such as MMP- 8, IL- 1β, TNF- α, and microRNA- 21 with high sensitiv- ity and specificity [ 192, 193]. Additionally, organic fluorescent probes, such as a coumarin- based “turn- on” sensor, have been designed to detect nitric oxide in human saliva, a molecule pres- ent in elevated concentrations in periodontitis patients, with de- tection limits in the nanomolar range [194]. While these specific examples may still not reach the level of diagnostic accuracy needed for large- scale clinical applica - tion, NP- based sensors could significantly enhance diagnostic potential by offering ultrasensitive detection of clinically rele - vant biomolecules [ 177, 195]. Integrating NPs into biosensing platforms—such as lateral flow assays and fluorescence- based systems—has the potential to enable rapid, point- of- care detec- tion of biomarkers in both GCF and saliva [191, 192, 196]. These advanced NPs- enabled diagnostic tools may facilitate diagnosis, possibly even through

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: otential to enable rapid, point- of- care detec- tion of biomarkers in both GCF and saliva [191, 192, 196]. These advanced NPs- enabled diagnostic tools may facilitate diagnosis, possibly even through integration with portable devices and smartphone technologies. 4.2 | Nanoparticles for the Prevention and Antimicrobial Treatment of Periodontitis While NPs demonstrate promising antimicrobial and immuno - modulatory efficacy in vitro, their effective local administration in clinical settings remains challenging due to the dynamic oral environment, as well as the anatomical complexity and limited accessibility of periodontal pockets. To understand the delivery strategies currently under investigation to overcome this hurdle, Table 1 summarizes clinical trials registered on clini caltr ials. gov, highlighting the different therapeutic formulations used, in- cluding particles, solutions, and injectable gels. Complementing these ongoing investigations, Table 2 presents outcomes from

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: r ials. gov, highlighting the different therapeutic formulations used, in- cluding particles, solutions, and injectable gels. Complementing these ongoing investigations, Table 2 presents outcomes from completed clinical studies, providing essential insight into the application of specific nanomaterials and their corresponding treatment efficacy. For example, in a pilot clinical study, NPs- assisted antimicro - bial photodynamic therapy (aPDT) was introduced to evalu - ate the efficacy of treating periodontitis [ 200]. In the study, methylene blue (MB) was loaded into PLGA NPs and admin - istered as mouthwash, followed by a 10- min irrigation of the periodontal pockets with MB solution. The pockets were then irradiated with 660 nm red light at an energy density of 20 J/ cm2. In recent years, various NPs- based materials such as drug- loaded polymer NPs, nHA, and bioactive glass have been investigated in clinical studies and demonstrated great efficacy in achieving regenerative outcomes (Table 2). 4.3.1 | NPs for Bone Regeneration Compared to open flap debridement (OFD) alone, the adjunctive use of nHA as a bone graft material led to statistically significant improvements over a 6 month period [201]. These improvements were observed in key clinical parameters such as GI, PPD, CAL, and gingival recession. However, bone defect area showed no significant change, suggesting limited

However, bone defect area showed no significant change, suggesting limited radiographic bone re - generation. Similarly, Bahammam et al. found that nHA with OFD did not significantly enhance bone density in periodontal intrabony defects unless combined with autologous platelet- rich fibrin (PRF) membranes [ 202]. Moreover, the combina - tion of nHA and PRF achieved the greatest PPD reduction and CAL gain. In contrast, Verardi et al. reported satisfactory clinical efficacy of using nHA as a bone graft for periodontal bone regeneration. In this study, intrabony defects were treated with a nHA/PLGA composite and then evaluated over a 12 month follow- up period (Figure 9B) [203]. However, more reliable, high- quality evidence is warranted to confirm these prelimi - nary findings. In addition to inorganic NPs, organic NPs, such as chitosan NPs, were also investigated in clinical trials (Figure 9C) [204]. These applications include the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of peri- implant diseases, as well as bone aug - mentation to support implant stability. Furthermore, NPs also facilitate implant surface modifications to enhance osseointe - gration and promote transmucosal healing. To achieve these clinical objectives, functional NPs are administered through multiple delivery approaches, as shown in Table 3. Notably, the two primary delivery strategies include surface coatings applied to implants and abutments and injectable gel formulations ad - ministered directly to the peri- implant sulcus. To validate these administration approaches, Table 4 presents the measurable outcomes from published clinical studies. These clinical data establish the translational potential of NP- based approaches in implant dentistry. 5.1 | Role in the Management of Peri- Implant Diseases Metal- based NPs coatings have been investigated for their dual

chunks.content: tablish the translational potential of NP- based approaches in implant dentistry. 5.1 | Role in the Management of Peri- Implant Diseases Metal- based NPs coatings have been investigated for their dual functions in promoting osseointegration while prevent - ing peri- implant diseases [ 217]. For example, in vitro data confirmed that AgNPs can reduce the bacterial load in dental biofilms and alter their formation dynamics [ 218, 219 ]. Once anchored onto titanium surface, AgNPs still demonstrated significant antibacterial properties against pathogens such as S. aureus in vitro, thereby assisting in the prevention of peri- implantitis [220]. More recently, AuNPs have been incor - porated in implant- retained overdentures to inhibit the forma - tion of microbial biofilms for preventive application [ 209]. This randomized clinical study evaluated 22 edentulous patients receiving mandibular overdentures retained by two implants, comparing conventional acrylic denture bases to AuNPs-

This randomized clinical study evaluated 22 edentulous patients receiving mandibular overdentures retained by two implants, comparing conventional acrylic denture bases to AuNPs- modified bases. Microbiological analysis of samples collected from implant necks and denture fitting surfaces revealed sig - nificantly reduced colonization by Candida albicans , E. coli , and Streptococcus mutans in the AuNPs- containing group at 2, 4, and 6 months post- placement, demonstrating sustained antimicrobial activity and potential for long- term prevention of peri- implant diseases. 5.2 | Nanoparticles for Enhancing Osseointegration As shown in Table 4, NPs- modified implant surfaces present promising potential in enhancing osseointegration. For ex - ample, a randomized clinical trial assessed titanium implants with various surface treatments, including bioabsorbable apa - tite nanocoating and sandblasted, acid- etched rough surfaces, and found that surface characteristics

Histological analysis revealed that implant surfaces with nanostructured calcium had the highest bone- to- implant contact values at 4 weeks. At 6 weeks, both roughened surfaces (SLA and XPEED) showed significantly higher values ( p < 0.05) than the MAC surface. At 6 weeks, it could be observed that there was diffuse contact osteogenesis along the implant surface and an increased amount of newly formed bone (Figure 10A). In another histological study of retrieved implant biopsies, the authors observed that the bone apposition rate, the speed at which new bone tissue is added to existing bone surfaces, was significantly faster around implants with the XPEED sur - face at 3 weeks and 5 weeks of healing, when compared to the SLA surface [ 221]. The results showed that nanostructured

chunks.content: ing bone surfaces, was significantly faster around implants with the XPEED sur - face at 3 weeks and 5 weeks of healing, when compared to the SLA surface [ 221]. The results showed that nanostructured calcium- incorporated surfaces could exhibit superior biocom - patibility and bioactivity compared to traditional surfaces. These clinical findings are consistent with the preclinical an - imal studies where nHA coated dental implants were able to strengthen bone quality and showed promise to improve the quality of osseointegration [ 222]. Recently, Granato et al. placed dental implants with a bioactive nanostructured CaP coated surface in the edentulous mandible of healthy and metabolic syndrome (MS) patients [211]. Further histological analysis of human retrieved samples demonstrated similar bone morphology and insignificant differences between these two groups regarding bone to implant contact values and the nanomechanical property of bone formed at the implant sur- face (Figure 10B).

These results indicated that nanoscale CaP particles can enhance osseointegration by promoting early bone healing and improving implant stability. Building on these promising clinical findings, several manu - facturers have translated nanotechnology- based surface mod - ifications into commercially available dental implant systems. In another split- mouth randomized clinical trial, nano- Ag coated healing abutments significantly reduced the accumulation of dental plaque on their surfaces in the oral cavity, which was demonstrated by a smaller plaque area compared to the uncoated pristine abutments in the same patients [34]. 6 | Challenges About Clinical Translation of Nanoparticle- Based Therapy 6.1 | Toxicity and Safety Concerns The small size and unique properties of NPs raise questions about their potential risks and long- term effects on human health and the environment. Due to their enhanced reactiv - ity, nanomaterials could pose toxicological hazards during manufacturing, use, and disposal [ 226]. For example, dental patients may encounter multiple potential exposures to NPs during periodontal and implant procedures,

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: uld pose toxicological hazards during manufacturing, use, and disposal [ 226]. For example, dental patients may encounter multiple potential exposures to NPs during periodontal and implant procedures, including di - rect contact with oral cells and tissues, accidental ingestion, and postoperative exposure of material to the oral cavity [227, 228 ]. Various studies have demonstrated that NPs can alter protein conformation, penetrate cellular membranes and further damage critical intracellular components such as mi - tochondria and DNA [ 229]. Although NPs in periodontal and dental implant applications are generally applied to a topical area, their potential for long- term accumulation, particularly for non- degradable NPs, raises significant toxicity concerns. Further studies are essential to understand these accumu - lation effects and to carefully balance therapeutic benefits against potential systemic risks. Moreover, while numerous studies have investigated how the physical and

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: tial to understand these accumu - lation effects and to carefully balance therapeutic benefits against potential systemic risks. Moreover, while numerous studies have investigated how the physical and chemical properties of nanomaterials affect cells and tissues, research specifically examining their interactions with oral- related cells and tissues remains limited. This gap is further compounded by methodological limitations in current toxicity assessments. Many in vitro models rely exclusively on animal- derived cells, which limits the generalizability of findings to human application. Similarly, in vivo studies using rodents and rabbits face translational challenges, as these spe - cies exhibit significantly different metabolic rates, immune systems, biofluid compositions, and microbial communities compared to humans. Therefore, research based solely on animal data cannot accurately capture the intricate interac - tion between NPs and the human oral environment, nor their potential

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: l communities compared to humans. Therefore, research based solely on animal data cannot accurately capture the intricate interac - tion between NPs and the human oral environment, nor their potential systemic distribution and effects throughout the body. To address these translational gaps, the development of advanced models for toxicity assessment such as organoids [230, 231] and computational models [ 232], is a critical priority for periodontal and dental implant research at the preclini - cal stage. 6.2 | Regulatory Barriers A product must be rigorously verified as effective for its intended clinical use or demonstrate greater efficacy than an existing product while also ensuring a high safety standard. The product can only possess the potential for significant clinical translation under these conditions [ 233]. Therefore, establishing clear and comprehensive guidelines for safety and efficacy from govern - ment and regulatory authorities is essential to this process [234]. In

chunks.content: n under these conditions [ 233]. Therefore, establishing clear and comprehensive guidelines for safety and efficacy from govern - ment and regulatory authorities is essential to this process [234]. In this regard, the recently proposed translational framework for nanomedicine serves as an excellent reference for consideration [233]. Moreover, there is a pressing need for further research on workplace exposure within the dental profession. Establishing comprehensive workplace regulations is essential to mitigate exposure risks and outline effective measures for reducing po - tential health hazards. 6.3 | Scalability and Cost Several technical and practical hurdles must be overcome be - fore these innovations can be widely adopted. Key challenges include: (1) achieving precise control over the physicochemical properties of NPs to minimize bench- to- bench variation; (2) preventing aggregation, which can compromise functionality in applications such as drug delivery and targeting; (3)

Furthermore, producing NPs in compliance with Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards significantly increases production costs, which remains a major barrier to clinical translation. chunks.content: 23 Journal of Periodontal Research, 2026 7 | Future Directions The successful integration of nanotechnology into periodon - tics and implant dentistry requires further multifaceted endeavors, including rigorous safety evaluation, continued in - novation in therapeutics and diagnostics, and strategic efforts to overcome regulatory and manufacturing barriers to clinical translation. 7.1 | Evaluating the Safety of Topically Applied Nanoparticles in the Oral Cavity While numerous studies have explored how nanomaterial properties affect cells and tissues, research specifically exam - ining interactions with oral cells and tissues remains scarce. To enhance the clinical relevance of safety assessments for periodontal and implant applications, studies investigating nano- bio interactions with oral cells and tissues, particularly those of human origin, are critically needed. Furthermore, research on NPs- tissue interactions has identified that bio - molecules, predominantly proteins, rapidly

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: ral cells and tissues, particularly those of human origin, are critically needed. Furthermore, research on NPs- tissue interactions has identified that bio - molecules, predominantly proteins, rapidly adsorb onto NP surfaces upon biological exposure, forming a layer termed the protein corona. Previous studies demonstrated that the com - position and abundance of protein coronas vary significantly depending on exposure to different biological fluids [ 236], as well as between in vivo and in vitro conditions [ 237–239]. This variability influences NP behavior in terms of cellular uptake, biodistribution, and targetability, thus raising critical concerns about both safety and therapeutic efficiency [ 231]. Therefore, investigations focused on the interactions between NPs and physiologically relevant oral fluids, such as saliva and GCF, and incorporating a dynamic microenvironment simulating the oral cavity (e.g., dynamic flow) have substan - tial transformative potential [ 240, 241 ].

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: ly relevant oral fluids, such as saliva and GCF, and incorporating a dynamic microenvironment simulating the oral cavity (e.g., dynamic flow) have substan - tial transformative potential [ 240, 241 ]. Another critical safety concern is whether topical application of nanomaterials in periodontology or implant dentistry results in systemic exposure, and how NPs distribute throughout the body. Under pathological conditions, capillary permeability increases significantly in both acute and chronic inflamma - tion, especially relevant in critical areas, such as periodonti - tis, peri- implantitis, and regenerative surgery. Additionally, patients with systemic diseases such as diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic viral hepatitis, etc. may exhibit enhanced inflammatory responses characterized by heightened endo - thelial permeability [ 242]. Periodontal pathogens, such as P. gingivalis , have been identified in circulating leukocytes and in atherosclerotic lesions, while others, such as F.

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: by heightened endo - thelial permeability [ 242]. Periodontal pathogens, such as P. gingivalis , have been identified in circulating leukocytes and in atherosclerotic lesions, while others, such as F. nucleatum , have been detected within the placenta [ 243]. If bacteria can traverse the endothelium during inflammatory responses, the considerably smaller NPs may exhibit similar or even greater translocation potential, raising critical questions about sys - temic toxicity. Given these safety considerations, comprehensive examina - tions of the interactions between NPs and oral endothelial cells under both physiological and pathological conditions, investigation of NP- immune interactions, biodistribution, metabolism, and long- term toxicological effects are essen - tial. To further bridge the preclinical- to- clinical gap, rigorously designed, large- scale, multi- centered randomized controlled trials are required to systematically evaluate the safety and therapeutic efficacy of NP- based interventions. 7.2 | Exploring Novel Nanoparticle- Assisted Therapeutics and Diagnostics Personalized approaches hold great promise for optimizing therapeutic outcomes, minimizing side effects, and accelerat - ing healing in periodontal and implant therapy. The importance of individualized strategies is exemplified by a study in which plasma samples from human subjects were used to investigate protein corona formation on NPs [ 244]. SDS- PAGE analysis revealed significant differences in the protein corona compo - sition between smokers and healthy individuals. Notably, even among healthy participants of the same gender and age group, the

Notably, even among healthy participants of the same gender and age group, the proteins adsorbed onto NPs exhibited remarkable variabil - ity, indicating that identical NPs designed in vitro may elicit di - vergent biological responses in vivo. These findings underscore the need for tailoring NP formulations to individual patient pro - files, including genetic, molecular, and environmental factors, to achieve more effective and targeted therapies [ 245]. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of diseases warranted adjust - able therapeutic profiles, as the microenvironment where NPs are applied can fluctuate over time, particularly in periodontal and peri- implant sites, both of which harbor diverse microbial communities. Additionally, the mechanisms via which antibac - terial NPs combat pathogens may also pose risks to host cells and tissue. Consequently, developing

Consequently, developing smart nanomaterials that target specific sites of interest and respond to key physiological cues, such as biomarkers, pH changes, ROS levels, and external stimuli, is paramount for achieving selective antimicrobial ac - tion while minimizing side effects. NPs are also opening new possibilities for diagnosing and man - aging periodontitis and peri- implantitis through non- invasive, real- time diagnostic tools. For example, NP- based biosensors ca- pable of detecting early signs of infection or inflammation [ 36] are particularly attractive from a clinical efficiency standpoint, as they simplify the diagnostic procedures and enhance patient comfort [ 246]. Despite these advances, broader obstacles such as reproducibil - ity issues, scalability to GMP standards, and regulatory uncer - tainty have hindered clinical translation of nanomaterials- based interventions. For successful clinical adoption, nanomaterial products must meet stringent criteria. They must be rigorously validated for their intended clinical use and demonstrate either equivalent efficacy to existing treatments with superior safety profiles or improved therapeutic outcomes while maintaining acceptable safety standards. To achieve these

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: cal use and demonstrate either equivalent efficacy to existing treatments with superior safety profiles or improved therapeutic outcomes while maintaining acceptable safety standards. To achieve these benchmarks, clear and com - prehensive regulatory guidelines from government and regula - tory authorities to standardize safety and efficacy assessments are essential [234]. In this context, the recently proposed trans - lational framework for nanomedicine provides valuable guid - ance for navigating the regulatory pathway [ 233]. Recent regulatory approvals offer encouraging precedent for nanotechnology in dentistry. In 2024, the FDA approved two antibacterial nanocoating products for orthopedic implants (Onkos Surgical and Orthobond), demonstrating the transla - tional potential of nanotechnology in clinical medicine [ 252]. These milestones suggest that with appropriate regulatory frameworks and rigorous validation, nanomaterial- based inter- ventions for periodontal and dental

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: nanotechnology in clinical medicine [ 252]. These milestones suggest that with appropriate regulatory frameworks and rigorous validation, nanomaterial- based inter- ventions for periodontal and dental implant applications could also progress from bench to bedside, ultimately revolutionizing disease management and treatment outcomes in dentistry. 8 | Conclusions The integration of NPs into periodontology and implant den - tistry represents a possible transformative advancement in the field. NPs' unique physicochemical properties, such as high sur - face area, tunable structure, and controlled degradability, allow for precise targeting of therapeutic agents, offering substantial improvements in infection control, implant success, and tissue regeneration. As highlighted in this review, NPs have demon - strated exceptional promise to promote osteogenesis and an - giogenesis, deliver antimicrobial agents, and enhance tissue healing, with several promising clinical studies in periodontol -

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: have demon - strated exceptional promise to promote osteogenesis and an - giogenesis, deliver antimicrobial agents, and enhance tissue healing, with several promising clinical studies in periodontol - ogy and implant dentistry. Moreover, the incorporation of diag - nostic capabilities into therapeutic NPs could enable real- time monitoring of the treated sites, allowing for adaptive treatment approaches that respond to the dynamic healing environment. However, translating these capabilities into clinical practice re - quires careful consideration of how multiple functionalities inter- act within complex biological systems. While preclinical studies have made great strides in developing multifunctional NPs that integrate diverse therapeutic activities to maximize outcomes, an important challenge has emerged: these functionalities may interact or compete within the complex periodontal and peri- implant microenvironment. For instance, multifunctional NPs designed to effectively combat

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: challenge has emerged: these functionalities may interact or compete within the complex periodontal and peri- implant microenvironment. For instance, multifunctional NPs designed to effectively combat pathogens and resolve inflamma- tion may inadvertently interfere with the ultimate goal of regener- ation. Antibacterial mechanisms can introduce potential toxicity to surrounding tissues, while excessive immunomodulation in - tended to enhance tissue repair may simultaneously suppress the immune responses necessary for pathogen clearance. These potential trade- offs highlight the critical need for sophisticated multifunctional NP platforms with optimized dosing strategies and sequential release profiles that can temporally and spatially harmonize antimicrobial, immunomodulatory, and regenerative functions. Beyond these functional considerations, substantial barriers continue to hinder their clinical application, especially in the aspects of safety, regulatory uncertainty, and

chunks.book_title: J of Periodontal Research - 2026 - Xu - Nanoparticles in Periodontology and Implant Dentistry  From Mechanisms to Clinical
chunks.content: and regenerative functions. Beyond these functional considerations, substantial barriers continue to hinder their clinical application, especially in the aspects of safety, regulatory uncertainty, and manufacturing limitations. To realize the full potential of nanotechnology in periodontal and implant dentistry, priority should be given to rigorous evaluation of the safety profiles of topically applied nanoparticles, including their interactions with oral tissues, potential for systemic translocation, and long- term biological effects. Building on this foundation, continued innovation in nanoparticle- assisted therapeutics and diagnostics will expand treatment options and enable precision medicine approaches. Emerging trends, such as the development of novel smart NPs and the application of AI offer exciting future directions that could enhance the clinical impact of NPs. These scientific ad - vances must then be supported by concerted translation efforts that address regulatory,

viii PREFACE The Moyers Symposium occupies a unique and distinguished place within the orthodontic and craniofacial biology community, serving as a cornerstone for scientific exchange and the advancement of clinical practice. Each year, this symposium draws together practitioners, researchers, educators, and students, united by a commitment to both the heritage and the forward momentum of the field. The Fifty-second Annual Moyers Symposium, held in Ann Arbor on March 1-2, 2025, continues this tradition, presenting a program purposefully centered on "Back to Basics." Amid a landscape inundated with enthusiasm and rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and technology, this meeting aims to connect the foundational principles of orthodontics with the latest research and contemporary clinical practice. It offers a thoughtful integration of proven methods and new discoveries, all anchored by scientific inquiry and a spirit of collegiality. In doing so, we reafﬁrm our dedication to

clinical practice. It offers a thoughtful integration of proven methods and new discoveries, all anchored by scientific inquiry and a spirit of collegiality. In doing so, we reafﬁrm our dedication to evidence-based, patient-centered care. As with tradition, the Symposium is preceded by the Annual International Conference on Craniofacial Research, known affectionately as "The Presymposium". This interdisciplinary gathering of researchers from all over the world further enriches the conversations and collaborations that the Moyers Symposium inspires. Our invited speakers represent a broad spectrum of expertise, spanning clinical practice, research, and ethics. This year’s discussions encompass historical perspectives and ethics, the critical importance of timing and prediction in growth and development, biomechanics, material science, retention and stability, current best practices in diagnostic imaging, and the prevention and management of orthodontic complications. The 52 nd Annual Moyers Symposium and the 49th Annual International Conference on Craniofacial Research were sponsored by the Department of Orthodontics and Pediatric Dentistry, School of Dentistry, University of Michigan. The proceeding of this annual meeting is memorialized in the 61st volume of the Craniofacial Growth Series and contains reports, original research, case series and review articles from internationally renowned experts, scientists and clinicians. CANINE IMPACTION: BACK TO THE BASICS WITH CLINICAL AND PERIODONTAL CONSIDERATIONS Bhavna Shroﬀ ABSTRACT Impa cted maxillary canines are observed in about 2% of the population. The treatment of impacted maxillary canines can be challenging and take longer to complete than the average treatment. The careful diagnosis of the position of an impacted canine has been facilitated by the introduction of three - dimensional (3D) imaging in orthodontics. The precise position of the canine and its relationship to the adjacent teeth can be easily visualized on a cone beam computed tomography ( CBCT). The presence of potential damage to the adjacent teeth can also be documented. Once the position of the canine has been determined, it is critical to determine the type of surgical exposure that will optimize the periodontal and esthetic outcomes of treatment. ptimize the periodontal and esthetic outcomes of treatment. In case of palatally impacted canines, an open exposure will facilitate the eruption of the tooth. In clinical situations where the tooth is labially impacted, an apically positioned flap is often recommended. The proper diagnosis and exposure technique of an impacted canine will help determine the appropriate mechanics that must be implemented. The analysis of the proper force system and the identification of undesirable side effects will expedite treatment and optimize the outcomes. KEY WORD S: Impacted canine, Biomechanics, Force system, Anchorage control INTRODUCTION Canine impaction is a challenging clinical situation for the orthodontist today. Maxillary impacted canines are observed in about 2% of the population and impaction of mandibular canines is rare compared to maxillary ones (0.35%) [1-3]. Most impaction of canines occurs in the palate (85%) and only 15% on the labial aspect of the maxilla [2, 3]. Girls are twice as likely to be more aﬀected as boys. Impacted canines are bilateral in 8% of cases and they are ﬁve times more common in Caucasians than in Asians [2]. Clinically, a lack of space on the arch is associated with labially impacted canines, whereas, palatally impacted canines generally have adequate space to erupt [2, 4]. The diﬃculties in treating patients presenting with impacted canines include some of the following factors: timing and accuracy of the diagnosis, availability of adequate imaging, surgical exposure and esthetic outcomes, length of treatment, and compliance of the patient. The treatment planning of these cases is complex, and the appropriate biomechanics need to be considered based on the correct diagnosis and treatment goals. The timing and accuracy of the diagnosis are critical factors that may help avoid the impaction of canines in some situations. Regular dental appointment s and follow up of the sequence of eruption are necessary in children starting at an early age. This allows for the early imaging of the maxillary canines and helps in determining the prognosis of a successful eruption of the maxillary canine. E arly detection of a potential canine impaction is critical because it will avoid subjecting a young patient to a challenging and lengthy treatment. Treating impacted canines often involves single or multiple surgical procedures and complicated mechanics which can be intimidating to a young child. The orthodontist must consider the information obtained from the clinical and 3D analysis and incorporate it in a list of detailed treatment goals. Some of the questions that need to be addressed during this phase include the following: • W here is the canine located with respect to surrounding teeth and how severe is the impaction? The diagnostic improvement brought by the introduction of 3D imaging has allowed the clinician to visualize the position of the canine and its proximity to other teeth, the potential damage already present to adjacent teeth (the lateral incisor speciﬁcally), and its height and angulation. This has been a game changer in the treatment of impacted canines. A detailed diagnosis allows for a precise treatment plan that can help expedite the treatment of a malocclusion that demands on average 6 to 9 extra months of therapy. It is therefore crucial that our approach to retention is evidence -based. Evidence -based retention means integrating research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient values. Case series A case series is a description of a group of patients treated with a particular type of treatment, or who present with the same outcome. There is no control group. This approach is often used when new techniques or materials have recently been developed and has been used to describe new types of retainers. The strength of evidence is weak, but is appropriately used to introduce new innovations, before they are later subjected to more robust research methods. Re trospective controlled study Thi s is the most common type of study in published retention research. The researchers look back at records to compare diﬀerent types of treatments. Th is type of study is relatively easy to organize and undertake, but it can suﬀer from potential bias, which may distort the ﬁndings of the research. There is a tendency for better records to be kept for patients whose treatment goes well, and if patients fail to complete treatment there may be no records at all. As a result, retrospective research tends to overestimate the outcomes of treatment. Ran domized controlled trials (RCTs) RC Ts are research studies where participants are randomly assigned to diﬀerent groups, one receiving a treatment or intervention (experimental group), and the other s receiving either a placebo, standard treatment, or no treatment at all (control group). The intervention is allocated randomly, so neither clinicians, nor patients, can choose which treatment they will receive. Randomization balances participant characteristics (both observed and unobserved) between the groups allowing attribution of any diﬀerences in outcome to the study intervention and reduces the eﬀect of confounding factors (both known and unknown). This ensures that the review process is transparent and can be replicated by others. Ther e is a recognized scientiﬁc approach to undertaking a systematic review: • identify a speciﬁc and clearly deﬁned question • use thorough and transparent search strategies to identify all relevant studies • critically appraise the studies for their quality and reliability • synthesize the ﬁndings of included studies to draw conclusions about the overall evidence on the research question. An increase in salivary flow rate, often observed during orthodontic treatment, is believed to enhance the buffering effect and facilitate the dilution of acid. PANORAMIC RADIOGRAPHS Panoramic radiographs are among the most commonly used extraoral imaging modalities in dentistry. They provide a broad overview of the maxillofacial region, including the teeth, jaws, temporomandibular joints (TMJs), and adjacent structures. Despite being a 2D representation of complex 3D anatomy, panoramic radiography remains a valuable tool for initial evaluation, treatment planning, and detecting abnormalities. A systematic, region-based approach ensures a comprehensive review, minimizing the risk of missing critical ﬁndings. 1. Indications Panoramic radiographs are indicated in a wide variety of clinical contexts. They are often used for initial orthodontic records and assessment, third molar evaluation, and dental age estimation and eruption

mic radiographs are indicated in a wide variety of clinical contexts. They are often used for initial orthodontic records and assessment, third molar evaluation, and dental age estimation and eruption patterns. Clinicians also utilize them for the detection of osseous pathology like cysts, tumors, or infections, and for the evaluation of trauma. While their use is limited, they can also assist in pre mini-implant assessment, TMJ screening, foreign body localization, and preliminary sinus evaluation. A lthough panoramic images have limitations in resolution and dimensional accuracy, they remain a ﬁrst-line imaging modality due to their low radiation dose, broad coverage, and quick acquisition time [5]. 2. Image characteristics Structures Flattened and Spread Out Panoramic radiographs project 3D structures onto a 2D image, where the buccolingual dimension is compressed, making it impossible to assess bone thickness and spatial relationships. Because of the curvilinear nature of the focal trough, some structures —especially those located along the curve of the dental arches—may appear ﬂattened, distorted, or spread out. This distortion can aﬀect structures such as the inferior nasal turbinates , which are anatomically located in the nasal cavity but spread out and superimposed onto the maxillary sinuses, making it diﬃcult to determine if the sinuses are clear. Similarly, the hard palate may be superimposed on the roots of maxillary teeth if the chin is positioned too high during image acquisition. Single and Double Images Panoramic radiography can produce either single or double images based on how the x-ray beam interacts with midline and bilateral structures. Single images are created when a structure lies within the path of the beam and is imaged only once, which

or double images based on how the x-ray beam interacts with midline and bilateral structures. Single images are created when a structure lies within the path of the beam and is imaged only once, which is typical in the case of the teeth and sinuses. Double images, however, occur when midline structures such as the soft palate, hyoid bone, epiglottis, or cervical spine are intercepted twice by the x-ray beam as it rotates, creating mirror-like duplicates. Some of these double images can be superimposed with the other anatomical structures, partially obscuring their visualization. For example, the double real images of the soft palate are partially superimposed with the rami, and the hyoid bone can be superimposed with the body of the mandible if the patient swallows during the scan. Real and Ghost Images Understanding the diﬀerence between real and ghost images is crucial for accurate interpretation. Real images are formed by structures located between the rotation center and the sensor . In contrast, ghost images occur when structures and objects, such as the mandible or earrings, lie between the x-ray source and the rotation center but outside the focal trough. These ghost images appear on the opposite side of the image from the real object, are typically projected higher up, and appear more magniﬁed, blurry, and closer to the midline . They are often seen with metallic accessories such as jewelry, hearing aids, or orthodontic bands. Clinically, ghost images can obscure anatomical structures and may compromise the diagnostic quality of the radiograph to the point that a retake may be necessary. These include the nasal and alar cartilage, the soft palate and uvula, the tongue (which can cause a palatoglossal air space if not pressed against the palate), and the ear lobe and tragus. Overlapping soft tissues, such as the soft palate and the ala of the nose, can sometimes mimic lesions as they increase the degree of radiopacity of the area where they are superimposed. Air Spaces Panoramic radiographs capture various air-ﬁlled spaces that appear radiolucent. Common air spaces include the palatoglossal air space (between the tongue and hard palate), the nasopharyngeal air space (behind the nasal cavity), the oropharyngeal air space (posterior to the oral cavity), and the glossopharyngeal air space (behind the tongue and pharynx). Zone 1: Dentition Within the dentition, clinicians should check for missing or supernumerary teeth, evaluate eruption patterns and developmental stage, and identify malpositions, rotations, and impactions or retained primary teeth. 5. Common pathologies detected on panoramic radiographs P anoramic radiographs are useful for detecting various common pathologies. These include odontogenic cysts (e.g., dentigerous cysts, radicular cysts), benign tumors (e.g., ameloblastoma, odontoma), and though far less common, primary or metastatic malignant lesions. They can also reveal developmental anomalies like cleidocranial dysplasia, and trauma such as fractures of the mandible, condyle, or zygomatic arch. Furthermore, panoramic radiographs are valuable for assessing pe riodontal bone loss (generalized or localized) and periapical pathology (chronic apical periodontitis). 6. LATERAL CEPHALOGRAM INTERPRETATION L ateral cephalometric radiography is a cornerstone of orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning. It allows clinicians to visualize craniofacial relationships in a sagittal and vertical dimension, offering reproducible landmarks critical for cephalometric analyses [6]. Despite its 2D limitations, cephalometry remains vital in assessing growth patterns, skeletal relationships, and anatomical variations that directly affect treatment planning and outcomes [7]. 1 . Clinicians rely on these images to evaluate growth patterns a nd make predictions about future development, monitor treatment progress throughout active therapy, assess post -treatment stability, and evaluate potential relapse requiring retreatment. The standardized nature of cephalometric imaging allows for precise measurements and comparisons that guide clinical decision- making throughout the entire treatment process. Image quality and technical considerations Before beginning any analysis, it is essential to ensure that the image is of diagnostic quality. The patient should be positioned in a natural head posture, with the teeth in centric occlusion unless otherwise specified. Ideally, the lips should be relaxed to allow for accurate assessment of soft tissue contours. It is also important to avoid motion blur and to verify that proper collimation and contrast have been achieved. While some degree of magnification may be present, the standardized projection geometry of lateral cephalometric radiographs generally ensures consistent and reproducible measurements. 3. The diagnostic process follows a structured, zone-based approach, moving systematically from top to bottom and anterior to posterior, ensuring that no critical ﬁndings are overlooked while maximizing diagnostic accuracy. Materials and Methods : A longitudinal sample of 144 Caucasian subjects with untreated Class III malocclusions was selected (80% training data; 20% test data). Cephalograms of the subjects of the test group were divided into short - and long-term observations. Sixteen cephalometric landmarks were digitized in a X Y Cartesian coordinate system. The trained model was a graph neural network (GNN). A one sample t-test and the Euclidean distances between predicted and observed values were calculated. Machine model design: data normalization and validation Given the semi-longitudinal nature of the available data and the relative paucity of the sample, it was necessary to use all available time intervals. The model was trained to predict the evolution of the coordinates for all time -ordered observations of an y given patient. Moreover, a small Gaussian noise was added to both training and test cephalometric points. For this reason, the X and Y coordinates in model output were an average of 10 predictions taken from 10 noise realizations. Normalization of coordinate values To normalize the coordinates, all 16 cephalometric points were set in a Cartesian axis with points X and Y for each cephalometric point (Figure 1). The X-axis was represented as a line passing through Nasion (N) with an angulation of 7° upwards with respect to the SN line, while the Y-axis was defined as a line perpendicular to X -axis and passing though Sella point. The origin of the Cartesian axis was SX = 0 and NY = 0. X and Y coordinates of cephalometric points were expressed in millimeters in all images. Algorithm training and testing To develop the predictive model, the sample was divided randomly into two groups: a training group and a testing group. The training group consisted of 80% of the subjects, selected randomly, while the remaining 20% constituted the test group. This distribution resulted in a training group comprising 116 subjects and a testing group comprising 28 subjects. The trained model was a graph neural network (GNN) consisting of one graph convolution layer (https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.029) [28] and one fully connected layer for prediction. All cephalometric coordinates on the X - and Y -axis (Fig ure 1) and three non -radiographic covariates were included as input variables. For each cephalometric point, the model received the following inputs: [X -axis coordinate, Y -axis coordinate, age, gender, and age of prediction] and produced outputs: [predicted X-axis coordinate, predicted Y-axis coordinate]. The model was tested for both short-term predictions (within 1.5 years from T0) and long-term predictions (more than 3 years from T0). The increase in Euclidean distances over time suggests that as individuals grow, the model faces greater difficulty in accurately forecasting cephalometric changes. Despite the limited predictability of mandibular points, Zhang et al. [38] developed an AI model to predict mandibular growth in children, using heat maps to enhance prediction accuracy. Their findings emphasized that AI primarily focuses on the chin, lower mandible, incisors, airway, and condyle—regions crucial for mandibular growth regulation [39]. Cephalometric landmarks detection is an operator- dependent procedure that is not free of interpretation by the operator, which can increase error [12]. Most existing AI studies on Class III malocclusion prediction have been conducted on Asian populations, while Caucasian samples remain underrepresented [27]. Understanding craniofacial growth variations across ethnic groups [ 40, 41] is essential for ensuring accurate predictions and generalizability. Additionally, many AI -based studies have focused on predicting growth up to adolescence, whereas research has shown that Class III malocclusions tend to worsen over time, particularly in males, up to age 21 [6]. Its success is measured not only by the achievement of facial symmetry and occlusal harmony, but also by the long-term stability of the skeletal and joint structures [1, 2]. and joint structures [1, 2]. A very important key factor in both the preoperative and post - operative phases is the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) [3]. Post -operative condylar remodeling — characterized by bone resorption, apposition, or deformation—can occur as a consequence of surgical repositioning and altered mechanical loading [5]. Even subtle shifts in condylar position can result in functional disturbances, discomfort, or degenerative changes over time. Therefore, careful evaluation and preservation of TMJ health is essential throughout the orthognathic treatment process. SKELETAL CLASS III MALOCCLUSION & TEMPOROMANDIBULAR JOINT S keletal Class III malocclusion is characterized by a sagittal discrepancy between the maxilla and mandible, in which the mandible is positioned anteriorly relative to the maxilla. This condition is often associated with maxillary hypoplasia, mandibular pr ognathism, or a combination of both [1]. Anatomically , patients may present with a concave facial proﬁle, a negative overjet, and an anterior crossbite, frequently accompanied by functional and aesthetic concerns. Surgical correction typically involves bimaxillary orthognathic surgery, which includes maxillary advancement —to reposition the maxilla anteriorly and improve midface projection— and mandibular

erns. Surgical correction typically involves bimaxillary orthognathic surgery, which includes maxillary advancement —to reposition the maxilla anteriorly and improve midface projection— and mandibular setback, to reduce mandibular protrusion and reestablish proper occlusion and facial balance [1, 2]. T he mandibular setback is most commonly performed using bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO), which allows for controlled repositioning of the distal mandibular segment. However, this procedure inherently involves manipulation of the proximal segment, which contains the mandibular condyles. Improper handling or misalignment of the proximal segments during surgery can lead to condylar displacement within the glenoid fossa, altering the normal biomechanics of the TMJ [5]. This fully automated protocol was applied to a sample of 17 skeletal Class III patients. After surgery, most patients showed minimal condylar remodeling (<1 mm) across the overall surface and individual poles. Patterns of condylar displacement included medial, posterior, and inferior shifts on both sides. Signiﬁcant correlations were found between regional bon e remodeling and condylar displacement, highlighting distinct remodeling behaviors at speciﬁc condylar regions following surgery. This syndrome is particularly concerning because it often encompasses multiple risk factors such as abdominal obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia (elevated cholesterol levels), and hyperglycemia (high blood sugar levels). Various studies have shown that those with metabolic syndrome are at a substantially greater risk for cardiovascular events and other health complications. Implementing lifestyle modiﬁcations—such as balanced healthy diets, exercise, stress management, and body weight control—can eﬀectively reduce the risk of developing more serious health issues linked to metabolic syndrome. These conditions are frequently associated with severe health complications, including heart disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, dementia, speciﬁc types of cancer, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease [4-7]. While the relationships between metabolic disorders and these health concerns are well established, it is imperative to emphasize some of the lesser -known risks associated with these disorders, such as the potential for birth defects, various bone diseases, and dry mouth, all of which can substa ntially impact oral health and the outcome of orthodontic treatment. A comprehensive understanding of these risks is essential for the maintenance of optimal bone and oral health, as they are integral to overall well-being and the eﬃcacy of orthodontic treatments. In particular, there is a speciﬁc relationship between cholesterol metabolism abnormalities and their eﬀects on bone and saliva production. Current research suggests that alterations in cholesterol metabolism can lead to decreased bone density and increase the risk of osteoporosis and fractures [10- 13] attributed to impaired osteoblast functions [14, 15], which are critical for bone repair and regeneration. Additionally, abnormal cholesterol levels may aﬀect the production and composition of saliva, diminishing its protective properties against dental caries and periodontal disease s, essential factors for maintaining oral health. Eﬀective management of metabolic diseases can be a safeguard of oral health and successful orthodontic outcomes. This chapter aims to highlight the importance of cholesterol metabolism in oral health, as a lesson from animal studies. BONES IN CHOLESTEROL METABOLISM ABNORMALITIES Nearly every cell within the human body is equipped with the primary cilium, a specialized cell surface structure that functions analogously to a cellular antenna [16]. This organelle is instrumental in the coordination of various cellular signaling pathways, the sensations of extracellular cues, and the execution of signal transduction processes [16]. The primary cilia play a critical role in osteoblast proliferation , osteogenic diﬀerentiation, and the maintenance of bone homeostasis [17-19]. Cholesterol, an essential lipid component of cellular membranes, is integral to the structural integrity and functional eﬃcacy of primary cilia [20, 21]. It contributes to the maintenance of membrane ﬂuidity, thereby facilitating eﬀective protein traﬃcking [22, 23] . Furthermore, cholesterol is essential for the formation of lipid rafts and caveolae —distinct microdomains

e maintenance of membrane ﬂuidity, thereby facilitating eﬀective protein traﬃcking [22, 23] . Furthermore, cholesterol is essential for the formation of lipid rafts and caveolae —distinct microdomains within the membrane that serve as organizational hubs for the assembly and interaction of signaling molecules [22, 23]. These microdomains are vital in initiating and regulating signal transduction events. Additionally, cholesterol becomes a source of several important biomolecules such as steroid hormones, oxysterols, and bile acids, emphasizing its multifaceted role in the body [24]. This cholesterol enrichment within primary cilia further underscores its critical importance in their structural dynamics. The synthesis of cholesterol is a multifaceted biochemical process involving numerous enzymatic reactions [25].
