In our recent studies, we found that mice deﬁcient in both Insig1 and Insig2 within cranial neural crest cells —essential cells making craniofacial structures—exhibit osteogenesis imperfecta [26]. Disturbances in these functions such as masticatory dysfunction and bruxism can lead to severe consequences including malocclusion, muscle pain, and temporomandibular disorders. Jaw movements are governed by the coordinated activity of the masticatory muscles innervated by the trigeminal nerve. Sensory feedback, particularly proprioception, which is the body’s ability to sense the position and movem ent, plays a critical role in modulating motor control. In the orofacial area, proprioceptive information is processed by the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (Vmes), a unique structure located in the brainstem. The Vmes receives the proprioceptive information from diﬀerent orofacial structures including the masticatory muscles, periodontal ligament, and temporomandibular joint (TMJ). Alterations in the proprioceptive signaling and processing can lead to disruption in the motor control of the masticatory muscles, aﬀecting the orofacial functions. However, the group II aﬀerents send more projections to the supratrigeminal nucleus, and weaker inputs to Vmotor, compared with the Ia aﬀerents [43]. Consequences of proprioceptive disruptions Tooth loss alters proprioception, aﬀecting the ﬁne control of masticatory muscles by altering the occlusal force magnitude, direction, and rate. K EY WORDS: Craniosynostosis, Suture, Biomaterial, Scaffold, Surgery INTRODUCTION D uring human growth and development, the immature calvaria begins its formation with the growth of five key bones. These five bones are the frontal and parietal bones (each of which are a pair of two bones) and the occipital bone [1]. Unlike many of the long bones of the human skeleton , which form via a process known as endochondral ossification, the cranial bones mature through the process of intramembranous ossification, whereby osteoblasts differentiate directly from mesenchymal cells [2]. Intramembranous bone formation begins as dense regions of mesenchymal cells begin to proliferate until a critical mass is reached. Once this occurs, the mesenchymal cells in the center of the growing cell population begin to

mation begins as dense regions of mesenchymal cells begin to proliferate until a critical mass is reached. Once this occurs, the mesenchymal cells in the center of the growing cell population begin to mature into osteoblasts. Eventually, the outer edge of the growing bones forms an osteogenic front. When growing cranial bones come into proximity with each other, a cranial suture is formed between the two adjacent osteogenic fronts. This suture tissue contains intermediate suture mesenchyme that is not mineralized and provides stem and osteoprogenitor cells needed for continued cranial bone growth [2, 3]. The establishment of cranial sutures occurs at approximately 18 weeks of prenatal development [4]. A cranial suture is defined as the mesenchymal soft tissue that lies in between the developing bones of the cranium [5]. The process of cranial growth occurs through an appositional mechanism whereby osteoid (pre -mineralized bony matrix) is deposited at suture margins [4]. It has been shown that, depending on the location of mesenchymal cells within the developing cranial suture, certain cells differentiate and certain cells do not. Those cells that differentiate into osteoblasts and become incorporated into the developing cranial bones are located at the edge of the suture, adjacent to osteogenic fronts [2]. In contrast, suture cells that are located within the middle of the suture remain undifferentiated, thereby preserving suture patency and a source of stem/progenitor cells. Furthermore, investigators have identified Gli1+ cells as the predominant population of stem cells within the suture mesenchyme [3]. Given the risk of premature suture fusion following an initial surgical intervention, it is desirable to implement a tissue engineering approach that can mitigate the possibility of secondary suture release surgeries for craniosynostosis patients. Langer and Vacanti cite Skalak and Fox, who described tissue engineering as a discipline that lies at the intersection of science and medicine, and ultimately aims to generate functional tissues in vivo as a means of treating various diseases [25-27]. There are several tissue engineering approaches that ultimately aim to restore normal biological function. The first approach involves purely the engineering and replacement of affected cell populations with subsequent replacement. The second strategy involves the delivery of substances, such as growth factors, which aim to induce tissue formation. First, recall that strip suturectomy procedures showed varying degrees of bony removal when creating the surgical defect. The protocol developed for this work allowed for material osseointegration to be analyzed without concerns regarding complete bony removal in the surgical defect, as placement of the defect in the right parietal bone allowed for easier and more consistent bony removal using the piezotome. Patients with DGI show dental defects including tooth discoloration, attrition, bulbous crown, pulp obliteration, and “shell teeth”. Shields proposed a classiﬁcation system with three types of DGI and two types of dentin dysplasia (DD) for hereditary dentin defects. With advancements in molecular genetics, researchers have found that non- syndromic DGI/DD (excluding DD-I) is exclusively caused by DSPP mutations. Findings in dental and genetic defects in DGI patients and molecular mechanisms in mouse models carrying human DSPP mutations indicate that 5’ and 3’ DSPP mutations cause diﬀerent types of DGI via distinct pathological mechanisms. Particularly, 5’ DSPP mutations cause both dentin and enamel defects, potentially due to endoplasmic reticulum stress in dentin- and enamel

diﬀerent types of DGI via distinct pathological mechanisms. Particularly, 5’ DSPP mutations cause both dentin and enamel defects, potentially due to endoplasmic reticulum stress in dentin- and enamel -forming cells. 3’ DSPP mutations cause severe dentin defects because of strong autophagy activities in dentin -forming cells. These insights facilitate the proposal of a revised Shields’ classiﬁcation and are critical for the development of molecular therapies that can precisely treat DGI according to the molecular mechanisms. Currently, multidisciplinary treatments are necessary for the management of DGI patients. Early interventions are preferred. MOLECULAR MECHANISMS With advancements in molecular biology technologies, the gene encoding dentin sialophosphoprotein (DSPP) was identiﬁed [12] and associated with DGI [13, 14]. Cumulative evidence indicates that DD-II, DGI- II, and DGI -III are exclusively caused by DSPP mutations. Mutations in genes causing osteogenesis imperfecta, including COL1A1 and COL1A2 that encode procollagen chains of type I collagen, may lead to DGI-I [15, 16]. Several genes have been associated with DD-I [17], although there is still ambiguity in associations of clinical features and genetic discoveries. By far, there have been more than 50 DSPP mutations that cause DD-II, DGI-II, and DGI-III reported in the literature [11, 18, 19] . These mutations can be primarily divided into two categories: 1) 5’ DSPP mutations, mostly missense or intronic mutations that will alter the amino acid sequence around the signal peptide cleavage site or the N -terminal targeting region, and 2) 3’ DSPP mutations, all of

P mutations, mostly missense or intronic mutations that will alter the amino acid sequence around the signal peptide cleavage site or the N -terminal targeting region, and 2) 3’ DSPP mutations, all of which are -1 frameshift (-1fs) mutations that change the hydrophilic DPP into hydrophobic mutant proteins [11]. There seems to be a correlation between DSPP mutations and DGI phenotypes, potentially via distinct molecular mechanisms. DSPP is predominantly expressed by odontoblasts (dentin-forming cells) and transiently expressed by ameloblasts (enamel-forming cells) [20, 21]. The two major DSPP cleavage products, dentin sialoprotein (DSP) and dentin phosphoprotein (DPP), were discovered long before the identiﬁcation of DSPP gene, because of their unique biochemical properties [22, 23]. DPP is the most acidic protein in humans with an isoelectric point of 1.1 [24]. DSP is a glycoprotein [23, 25]. Proteoglycan forms of DSP are also identiﬁed [26-29]. The acidity of DPP and the carbohydrate units on DSP may be essential for dentin mineralization. Mice without DSP and DPP develop limited mineralized dentin: large areas of the dentin matrix remain unmineralized as predentin [21, 30]. Mice without DPP show hypomineralized dentin globules [21, 31]. Neither mouse shows dentin defects in heterozygous conditions. Dental pulps of mice without DSP and/or DPP do not get obliterated over time [30, 32]. The molecular pathological mechanisms of DGI have been further explored using DsppP19L and Dspp- 1fs mice [36]. In both types of mice, DSPP proteins accumulate in odontoblasts and ameloblasts. The secretion of DSPP is also impaired in odontoblasts of DsppP19L mice, with most DSPP proteins remaining in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) that cause ER stress [33, 36] . Although DSPP proteins also accumulate in the ameloblasts of Dspp-1fs mice, the cellular retention of DSPP proteins is relatively brief, causing minimal enamel defects, if any, in Dspp-1fs mice [33, 36]. Therefore, a revised Shields’ classiﬁcation has been proposed based on genetic mutations [11]. First, 5’ DSPP mutations usually lead to both enamel and dentin developmental defects. The enamel and dentin defects are most likely caused by ER stress in ameloblasts and odontoblasts. SUMMARY D GI is the most common inherited dentin disorder. Except for DD -I, which is characterized by short roots, non-syndromic DGI is exclusively caused by DSPP mutations that can be primarily categorized into two types: 5’ and 3’ DSPP mutations. Findings in both human patients with DGI and mouse models carrying human DSPP mutations indicate that the dental defects resulting from these two types of DSPP mutations and the molecular mechanisms underlying these two types of DSPP mutations are distinct. These ﬁndings facilitate the diﬀerential diagnosis and the development of precise molecular therapeutic options based on DSPP mutations. M anual segmentation, considered the most direct method for segmenting medical images, involves tracing anatomical structures in each image slice. By defining a region of interest (ROI) in each section, it is possible to construct a volume of interest through the sequential merging of these delineated regions. This approach proves particularly valuable in complex scenarios, such as those involving low-resolution images, the presence of artifacts, or intricate anatomical morphologies. By providing precise delineations in two-dimensional (2D) or 3D images, manual segmentation enables not only the 3D reconstruction of anatomical structures but also the volumetric measurement of relevant tissues [15]. The resulting average variation ranged from 2.5% to 3.5%, demonstrating high reproducibility and no statistically significant difference between operators [16]. CONCLUSIONS T he progressive integration of AI into dental imaging has transformed the segmentation of dento- maxillofacial structures, particularly in CBCT. This chapter demonstrated the evolution from labor - intensive manual segmentation methods to increasingly robust and efficient automated techniques, emphasizing their application in pediatric patients with developing dentitions. While manual and semi-automatic methods remain essential for validation and refinement, deep learning -based segmentation models , such as Ped iatricDentalSegmentator, have shown high accuracy and consistency. These tools not only reduce segmentation time dramatically but also improve accessibility through open-source deployment, addressing critical needs in both research and clinical contexts. N C left lip and/or palate (CLP) are the most common craniofacial anomalies, resulting from a failure in the fusion of facial prominences during early embryogenesis [1]. The global incidence of CLP is estimated at approximately 1.7 per 1,000 live births, with notable geographic variation [2] . The etiology of CLP is multifactorial, involving a combination of genetic and environmental factors [3-5]. Complete clefts extend through the lip, alveolus, and palate, while incomplete clefts may involve only a subset of these structures. CLP can also be c lassified as unilateral or bilateral and may occur in isolation (non -syndromic) or as part of a syndrome (syndromic) [6]. The presence of an alveolar cleft disrupts the continuity of the maxillary arch, affecting dental development and craniofacial growth. Teeth adjacent to the cleft —particularly the lateral incisor and canine—often present with abnormal positioning or impact ion due to the lack of bon y support [7]. This discontinuity also compromises masticatory function, nasal floor integrity, and midfacial development , leading to malocclusion, transverse maxillary collapse, and facial asymmetry. Additionally, the persistence of an oronasal fistula may impair speech and nasal airflow, further complicating rehabilitation [8]. Effective management of CLP requires a multidisciplinary approach, integrating the expertise of plastic surgeons, oral and maxillofacial surgeons, orthodontists, speech -language pathologists, psychologists, and other professionals [9]. Secondary alveolar bone grafting (SABG) is performed during the mixed dentition stage (9–12 years), prior to the eruption of the permanent canine [ 10-12]; furthermore, other protocols and timings may also be applied achieving the success [13]. ABG provides maxillary stabilization, closure of oronasal fistulas, nasal base support, periodontal health, and facilitates orthodontic and prosthetic rehabilitation [7, 14]. T he iliac crest has traditionally been the gold standard donor site due to its abundant cancellous bone. However, it is associated with donor site morbidity, including postoperative pain, gait disturbances, and non-aesthetic scar [15]. In contrast, the mandibular symphysis has emerged as an alternative donor site due to its proximity, ease of access, and lower morbidity. Studies have

, gait disturbances, and non-aesthetic scar [15]. In contrast, the mandibular symphysis has emerged as an alternative donor site due to its proximity, ease of access, and lower morbidity. Studies have reported comparable success rates between mandibular symphysis and iliac crest bone in achieving bone formation [15-26] and supporting spontaneous tooth eruption through the grafted area [21, 27]. The symphyseal approach is performed intraorally, avoiding external scars, and provides sufficient bone for unilateral clefts [15-26]. T he evaluation of ABG outcomes has significantly advanced with the use of cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), which enables comprehensive three-dimensional (3D) visualization of the cleft area, and the bone bridge formed in the alveolus . CBCT enables high -resolution analysis, allowing precise quantification of bone formation and measurement of buccopalatal and vertical dimensions of the new bone bridge —overcoming the limitations of conventional two

h -resolution analysis, allowing precise quantification of bone formation and measurement of buccopalatal and vertical dimensions of the new bone bridge —overcoming the limitations of conventional two -dimensional (2D) imaging, which often underestimates graft outcomes due to projection distortion and anatomical overlap [ 25, 28, 29]. When enhanced with artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools, CBCT further improves reproducibility and enables automated, detailed evaluations of graft success [30]. This pilot study aimed to assess ABG outcomes using mandibular symphysis bone and to investigate donor site healing dynamics through a novel AI - enhanced 3D assessment protocol. DISCUSSION T he integration of CBCT with AI -based tools has significantly advanced the evaluation of ABG outcomes. Unlike conventional 2D radiographs—limited by projection distortions and lack of volumetric detail [12, 25, 28, 33]—CBCT provides high -resolution 3D data. When enhanced by AI -driven segmentation, this approach improves the efficiency, reproducibility, and

distortions and lack of volumetric detail [12, 25, 28, 33]—CBCT provides high -resolution 3D data. When enhanced by AI -driven segmentation, this approach improves the efficiency, reproducibility, and objectivity of volumetric assessments, achieving a level of precision comparable to that of expert clinicians [34]. Preliminary CBCT analysis of this subsample revealed consistent reductions in cleft width postoperatively, with near- zero values at the apical level—indicating not only successful graft integration but also the sensitivity of this AI integrated methodology to detect subtle morphological changes. Notably, the individualized segmentation of anatomical structures enabled accurate measurements even in cases with teeth in the cleft region. The variability observed in pre - and postoperative cleft dimensions re flects the inherent anatomical heterogeneity of cleft morphology [35, 36], rather than methodological inconsistencies. This individualized, image -guided analysis can support more precise clinical decision- making and may contribute to optimized treatment strategies, potentially improving outcomes and long-term care for each patient. Th e preliminary ABG outcomes support the effectiveness of mandibular symphysis bone as a reliable graft source for cleft reconstruction. The reconstructed alveolar ridge demonstrated notable buccopalatal thickness, mesiodistal extension, and vertical height—parameters considered essential for functional and anatomical success [12, 13, 21, 25, 26, 31]. Despite the symphyseal region offering smaller graft volumes compared to the iliac crest, it was sufficient for achieving almost full defect closure in this cohort. Furthermore, harvesting from the mandibular symphysis results in less morbidity, faster recovery, and shorter hospitalization periods when compared to extraoral donor sites [37]. M oreover, the presence of a robust and continuous bone bridge plays a central role in the multidisciplinary rehabilitation of patients with CLP . Grafted alveolar ridges serve as a foundation for future prosthodontic interventions, including dental implants, which demonstrate success rates comparable to those placed in non- cleft patients [ 38, 39]. Thus, the bone morphology achieved in this study not only fulfilled immediate reconstructive goals but may also lay the groundwork for long-term functional and esthetic rehabilitation. H ealing at the mandibular symphysis donor site was favorable, with no adverse clinical outcomes. Although concerns have been raised regarding potential effects on mandibular growth, facial contour, and future genioplasty, current longitudinal evidence indi cates that symphyseal bone harvesting does not significantly impact mandibular development or chin projection [24, 40]. When present, minor contour alterations are transient and fall within the range of normal physiological remodeling [4 0]. In this cohort, the residual bone was minimal (2.7 ± 1.4 mm), and no cases of pulpal or sensory impairment were noted, reinforcing the symphyseal region as a probable safe and reliable autogenous donor site for alveolar cleft reconstruction. T his p reliminary study, which is part of an ongoing clinical investigation, confirmed the methodological feasibility of using mandibular symphysis bone for alveolar cleft reconstruction. Despite the small sample size, the use of a standardized surgical protocol, consistent execution by a single experienced surgeon, and the integration of AI-enhanced 3D imaging analysis provided a solid framework for assessing outcomes related both to alveolar bone formation and regeneration at the donor site. These preliminary findings support the viability of the proposed methodology and justify its continued application in subsequent phases of the trial, which will incorporate comparative groups involving alternative autogenous graft sources and adjunctive biomaterials. The notable bone bridge formation supports the mandibular symphysis as a viable donor site for ABG in patients with unilateral CLP, justifying its continued assessment and validation of reproducibility in the larger cohort of this ongoing RCT. EARLY TREATMENT OF PATIENTS WITH ANTERIOR OPEN BITE WITH BONDED SPURS Aron Aliaga del Castillo, Gabriela Utrago, Silvio Augusto Bellini-Pereira, Camila Massaro, Felícia Miranda, Lorena Vilanova, Guido Marañón-Vásquez, Luis Ernesto Arriola-Guillén, Marilia Yatabe, Antonio Ruellas, Lucia Cevidanes, Daniela Garib, Guilherme Janson (in memorium) ABSTRACT Anterior open bite (AOB) is often associated with increased lower anterior face height. Some early treatment protocols use appliances that allow vertical dentoalveolar development of the anterior teeth without interference (i.e., control of deleterious habits) with those that help control the vertical dimension. This chapter discusses the results of a clinical trial that compared the dentoalveolar and skeletal effects of bonded spurs associated with build -ups versus only bonded spurs in the early treatment of AOB. Forty-nine children aged between 7 and 11 years with AOB were prospectively and randomly allocated in either the experimental

ed with build -ups versus only bonded spurs in the early treatment of AOB. Forty-nine children aged between 7 and 11 years with AOB were prospectively and randomly allocated in either the experimental group (24 patients treated with bonded spurs associated with build-ups, 17 female, 7 male; mean age of 8.22+1.06 years) or the comparison group (25 patients treated with bonded spurs, 14 female; 11 male; mean age of 8.30+ 0.99 years). Lateral headfilms and digital dental models were obtained at baseline (T1) and after 12 months of follow-up (T2). Both protocols were demonstrated to be effective in early treatment of AOB, without significant differences. Therefore, bonded spurs alone represent a practical and efficient option for the early treatment of AOB with simplified clinical protocols and effective outcomes. KEY WORDS: Open bite, Orthodontic appliance, Bonded spurs INTRODUCTION Anterior open bite (AOB) is defined by the absence of vertical contact between the upper and lower incisors while posterior teeth remain in occlusion [1, 2]. AOB is considered one of the most challenging malocclusions to treat in the permanent dentition, as the treatment often involves more complex and less stable orthodontic interventions [1, 2]. This vertical discrepancy can lead to functional problems, such as difficulties in incising food and pronouncing certain phonemes [3 -5]. In addition, AOB can lead to esthetic concerns affecting the facial profile and the smile [3-5]. As a result, patients with AOB may experience psychosocial issues, including socialization difficulties, which can negatively affect their quality of life [3 -5]. Therefore, early inter vention of AOB offers several advantages, such as preventing the establishment of deleterious habits, promoting normal dentoalveolar development, reducing the need for more invasive procedures in the future, and improving the patient’s self-esteem and overall quality of life during growth and development [6, 7]. Th e prevalence of AOB in the mixed dentition is 17% [8, 9]. The etiology of AOB is considered multifactorial, involving genetic and environmental factors [1, 9, 10]. Deleterious oral habits, such as pacifier or thumb sucking, tongue thrusting, and mouth breathing represent the most common environmental factors associated with AOB [9, 10]. The establishment of AOB depends not only on the presence of deleterious oral habits, but also on their frequency, duration, and intensity, as described by Graber’s triad [11]. This association is so strong that both prolonged sucking habits and hyperdivergent vertical skeletal relationships significantly increased the probability of developing AOB, with prevalence rates reaching up to 36.3% [9]. W hen the malocclusion is caused by deleterious habits, it is classified as dentoalveolar AOB, which generally has a good treatment prognosis if the causal factors are eliminated [1, 9, 10, 12]. Even bone tissue, despite being structurally strong, can become malleable when subject to prolonged and low-intensity forces, inhibiting incisors’ dentoalveolar vertical development and resulting in AOB [11]. On the other hand, when AOB is related to genetic factors, it is classified as skeletal AOB [12]. These features predispose to an increased gonial angle, generating clockwise mandibular rotation and an increase in lower anterior facial height [2, 10, 13]. The greater the influence of genetic factors, the poorer the treatment prognosis [2, 10, 13]. S ome treatment protocols for early management of AOB have been described with effective results, such as fixed or removable palatal cribs and bonded spurs [14-24]. Success rates ranging from 53.8% to 86.7% for bonded spurs [14, 15, 17, 18, 22, 24, 25] and from 74% to 100% for palatal cribs have been demonstrated [16-21, 23, 24]. The gold standard for treating dentoalveolar AOB in the mixed dentition is the fixed palatal crib [16 -20]. This device acts as a mechanical barrier, preventing the execution of deleterious oral habits, promoting the vertical development of the incisors, and consequently correcting the dentoalveolar AOB [16-21]. The palatal crib can be fixed or removable, but the main disadvantage of removable appliances is the need for patient compliance to achieve successful outcomes [17]. Therefore, the fixed appliance is generally preferred [16]. Furthermore, the muscular imbalance between intraoral and perioral musculature caused by deleterious oral habits can lead to transverse discrepancy, such as posterior crossbite [27]. Bo nded spurs placed in the palatal and lingual surfaces of upper and lower incisors, respectively, can be considered an effective alternative for early treatment of AOB [14, 15, 17, 18, 22, 24, 25]. They offer some advantages, including low cost, small size, good esthetics, no need for laboratory preparation, easy installation, and reduced chair time [14, 18, 24]. A OB is often associated with a vertical growth pattern and increased anterior facial height [2, 9, 10]. If left untreated, this relationship may worsen with age, leading to more severe malocclusion [10, 29, 30]. Therefore, protocols that combine abandonment of deleterious oral habits with vertical dimension control have been proposed [15, 17, 23, 24]. The main objective of these therapies is to promote counterclockwise mandibular rotation by controlling or intruding the posterior teeth [15, 17, 23, 24]. Therefore, a question arises: could combining bonded spurs with posterior build-ups on the upper deciduous and first permanent molars potentially enhance AOB correction compared to bonded spurs alone in the mixed dentition? If so , this improvement may result in mandibular counterclockwise rotation following posterior intrusion, offering a fixed, hygienic, and patient-compliance-independent alternative for vertical control. METHODS To evaluate this hypothesis, a randomized clinical trial was conducted at Bauru Dental School, University of São Paulo, to compare the changes produced by bonded spurs combined with posterior build-ups versus conventional bonded spurs in the early treatmen t of AOB [32 -36]. The study was approved by the Ethics in Research Committee of this institution, and informed consent was obtained from all patients and their parents or legal guardians. Patient recruitment was performed from June 2017 to April

he Ethics in Research Committee of this institution, and informed consent was obtained from all patients and their parents or legal guardians. Patient recruitment was performed from June 2017 to April 2018. The inclusion criteria were: patients aged between 7 and 11 years, AOB > 1 mm (clinically evaluated as the vertical distance between the incisal edges of the maxillary and mandibular central incisors), erupted first permanent molars, with the maxillary and mandibular permanent central incisors fully erupted, without or with only mild crowding, and without the need for maxillary expansion. Children with previous orthodontic treatment, craniofacial anomalies or syndromes, tooth agenesis, loss of permanent teeth, severe crowding, maxillary constriction, or posterior crossbite were excluded. The success rate was 66.7% (16 of 24 patients) in the experimental group and 72% (18 of 25 patients) in the comparison group. Previous studies have reported success rates of 86.7% with bonded spurs combined with high-pull chin cup therapy [15], 16% to 86.6% with fixed lingual spurs alone [14, 22], and 53.8%, 80%, and 84.5% with bonded spurs alone [14, 17, 18]. The success rates reported in the present study are consistent with these previous findings, demonstrating that most patients achieved a positive overbite after AOB early treatment. Comparable or higher success rates have been observed for palatal cribs, which can be attributed to the extensive blocked area for tongue projection, thumb, or pacifier [18]. Nevertheless, factors such as the need for laboratory fabrication, longer chairside time, and higher costs should be considered, compared to bonded spurs [14, 18]. Although accidental ingestion and tongue irritation are commonly reported as side effects of bonded spurs therapy [39], no adverse effects were observed in this study. Debonding of bonded spurs and build-ups occurred in 2.5% and 5.3% of cases, respectively, but these were easily repositioned without significant complications. Therefore, the selection of the appropriate treatment protocol should consider the patient’s initial clinical characteristics, the orthodontist’s preferences, and a careful evaluation of the advantages and disadvantages of each protocol. Limitations of the study The main limitation of the present study was the absence of an untreated control group of AOB patients to compare with normal growth, which was not feasible for ethical reasons. In addition, the short follow -up period of 12 months was insufficient to evalu ate long -term stability or achieve complete open bite closure in all cases, especially in the presence of persistent oral habits and greater vertical skeletal involvement. ESTHETIC ALTERNATIVE FOR ANTERIOR OPEN BITE TREATMENT IN THE MIXED DENTITION Camila Massaro, Gabriela Utrago, Amanda Marques, Lourival Garcia, Aron Aliaga-del Castillo, Lucia Cevidanes, Daniela Garib ABSTRACT Anterior open bite (AOB) is a malocclusion characterized by the lack of vertical overlap between the upper and lower incisors when the posterior teeth are in contact. It can affect masticatory function, speech, and smile esthetics, influencing the child’s self- perception and social integration. Early treatment during the mixed dentition phase is recommended with the potential of improving the quality of life of patients. Among the therapeutic options for early AOB intervention, removable appliances such as the high -pull chin cup and removable palatal crib are used, but their success depends on patient compliance. The fixed palatal crib is widely recognized as the gold standard for interceptive treatment of AOB, effectively promoting bite closure by mechanically preventing

success depends on patient compliance. The fixed palatal crib is widely recognized as the gold standard for interceptive treatment of AOB, effectively promoting bite closure by mechanically preventing tongue thrust and discouraging habi ts like thumb sucking. This chapter introduces the Esthetic Palatal Crib (Ice Crib), an innovative fixed appliance that combines the classic metallic palatal structure with transparent extensions in the anterior region , enhancing esthetic and social accept ance without compromising therapeutic effectiveness. Preliminary results show promising outcomes in AOB closure and habit cessation with the Esthetic Palatal Crib. In addition, good acceptance was reported by the first patients to receive the appliance. Further studies will continue to evaluate the clinical outcomes of the Esthetic Palatal Crib, aiming to support its integration into orthodontic practice. W hen properly indicated, interceptive orthodontic treatment may simplify or even eliminate the need for a second intervention [1, 2]. In this context, anterior open bite (AOB) deserves our attention. This malocclusion is defined by the lack of vertical contact between anterior teeth, while the posterior teeth are in occlusion, resulting in a negative overbite [3, 4]. The negative impact of this condition on children’s quality of life [5], as well as the prove n benefit of early treatment when indicated [6, 7], make this topic of great relevance in orthodontics. A comprehensive understanding of the etiology and clinical characteristics of AOB is essential for accurate diagnosis,

A comprehensive understanding of the etiology and clinical characteristics of AOB is essential for accurate diagnosis, appropriate selection of a suitable therapeutic intervention, and determination of the ideal timing for treatment. The etiology of AOB is considered multifactorial, and may be related to genetic factors, environmental influences, or a combination of both [3, 8] . The persistence of deleterious oral habits, such as thumb or pacifier sucking and tongue thrusting, is a major etiological factor in this condition [3, 8]. When the AOB is primarily caused by persistent non -nutritive sucking habits, it generally presents a dentoalveolar pattern with a favorable treatment prognosis and post - treatment stability, if the etiological factor is removed [8]. In contrast, when the etiology is skeletal and genetically determined, the condition tends to be more complex and less pred ictable [3].

Additionally, airway obstruction and mouth breathing must be considered during the etiological investigation of AOB [3]. In such cases, referral to an otolaryngologist should precede orthodontic intervention. I n the deciduous dentition, t he prevalence of AOB is approximately 27% among children with non-nutritive sucking habits [9]. In the mixed dentition, AOB affects approximately 18% of children [8, 10, 11] . In the presence of non-nutritive sucking habits and /or a vertical growth pattern, this prevalence increases to 36.3% [8]. The decrease in the prevalence of AOB from deciduous to mixed dentition phase can be explained by the spontaneous correction of the overbite after the abandonment of such habits [12]. P revious studies showed that AOB can affect not only masticatory and speech function but also smile esthetics, influencing self-perception and potentially impacting social integration and quality of life [13, 14] . This highlights the importance of appropriate early intervention , beginning from the mixed dentition stage [12]. In the following sections of this chapter, we will review the literature on early treatment of AOB and introduce the initial clinical outcomes of a novel esthetic alternative for this approach [12, 15]. Interestingly, this was demonstrated in previous studies assessing the OHRQoL after orthodontic treatment with different protocols [6, 7]. The interceptive treatment of AOB plays a critical role by helping to eliminate persistent deleterious oral habits, correct tongue posture, guide proper tooth positioning, and support normal dental development [16]. These measures not only improve function and esthetics but also contribute to the long- term stability of treatment outcomes [16-20]. A variety of options are available for AOB treatment, including fixed palatal crib, bonded spurs, high-pull chin cup, and removable palatal crib [18]. The fixed palatal crib (Figure 1) is a classic device traditionally used in the management of deleterious oral habits in orthodontics. First described in the mid-1940s, [21, 22] it remains the gold standard to this day. Figure 1. Fixed palatal crib. A) Frontal View, B) Occlusal view. As a result, the habit becomes unrewarding and is typically abandoned [23]. These arches were connected by small transverse segments of 0.045 -inch wire, forming a grid- like structure that acted as a physical barrier [23]. Although the design of the fixed palatal crib remains similar today, the gold wire has been replaced with stainless steel, offering greater durability and cost- effectiveness. The design of the appliance can be modified in the presence of transverse discrepancies [17, 19]. In individuals with non -nutritive sucking habits, such as pacifier or thumb sucking, the tongue often remains in low position and may be unable to apply the necessary pressure against the palate for transverse maxillary arch growth [24, 25]. Moreover, in an attempt to achieve an anterior seal, which is compromised due to the presence of a negative overbite, the tongue tends to adopt an abnormal posture at rest and during swallowing [16]. This dysfunctional posture impairs normal tongue function and may also contribute to the development or persistence of transverse discrepancies [24, 25] . Therefore, the use of a Q uad-Helix appliance in combination with palatal crib represents a viable treatment option in such cases, as it addresses both the vertical and transversal discrepancies [17, 19]. The fixed palatal crib is a passive device [16, 23], which acts as a mechanical barrier, preventing the persistence of deleterious oral habits [16, 23]. As a result, the anterior teeth undergo extrusion along with the alveolar process until a positive overbite is passively achieved [16, 17, 19, 20, 26, 27]. In addition to the vertical changes, the maxillary and mandibular incisors exhibit lingual tipping, contributing to relative extrusion that further facilitates AOB closure [16, 17, 19, 20, 27]. ndibular incisors exhibit lingual tipping, contributing to relative extrusion that further facilitates AOB closure [16, 17, 19, 20, 27]. Several studies have demonstrated favorable long-term stability after AOB correction with fixed palatal cribs during the mixed dentition [16-20]. Reported stability rates ranged from 80% to 100% in treatment performed during the mixed dentition [16-20]. In contrast, stability rates in the permanent dentition are lower, ranging from 62% to 75%, and typically required more complex interventions [28, 29]. The greater stability observed in early treatment may be attributed to the elimination of deleterious oral habits that act as mechanical barriers to vertical development of anterior teeth [16- 20]. These findings support the clinical effectiveness of fixed palatal cribs in allowing anterior vertical development of incisors and in disrupting harmful habits, contributing to long-term stability [16-20]. Bonded spurs are also indicated for the early treatment of AOB [7, 18, 26, 27] . This alternative offers some advantages, including low cost, improved esthetics, elimination of the laboratory phase, a simplified technique, and reduced chair time [18, 27]. Bonded spurs are attached to the lingual surfaces of the incisors rather than supported by molar bands, as seen with fixed palatal cribs [7, 26]. Despite the benefits, bonded spurs tend to be less effective in correcting AOB [27] and in eliminating persistent oral habits [18]. Additionally, bonded spurs demonstrated some disadvantages such as frequent debonding during treatment [27]. In children, especially in those with persistent sucking habits, fixed appliances are generally preferred, as they do not rely on patient cooperation. Currently, there is increasing demand for more esthetic and discreet orthodontic appliances [30]. Esthetic concerns during interceptive orthodontic treatment should also be considered, as many patients may face bullying, embarrassment, or negative comments in the school environment [13, 30]. enefiting both patients and clinicians. CONCLUSIONS Early treatment of AOB is recommended during the mixed dentition phase. This intervention should be coordinated within an interdisciplinary team and involve the selection of the most effective appliance to promote AOB closure. The fixed palatal crib remains the gold standard for early treatment in this stage. The Esthetic Palatal Crib was introduced as a fixed and esthetic alternative, designed to enhance patient acceptance and social well- being without compromising the effectiveness of interceptive orthodontic treatment. Preliminary results are promising, and further studies will continue to evaluate its clinical outcomes, aiming to support its integration into orthodontic practice. K EY WORDS: Dental occlusion, Orthodontics, Non-syndromic cleft, Dental arch INTRODUCTION P atients with unilateral cleft lip and palate (UCLP) present clinical challenges that require nuanced, individualized treatment planning and evaluation. The dental anomalies , ranging from malocclusion to alterations in dental arch form, combined with maxillofacial discrepancies, impose complex demands not routinely encountered in conventional orthodontics. In many cases, comprehensive care extends from the early mixed dentition period through to post -surgical rehabilitation, necessitating an orthodontic assessment tool that can capture both gross occlusal discrepancies and subtle reﬁnements following therapy [1]. METHODOLOGY S tudy design and sample selection A retrospective study design was employed to test the validity and reliability of the COR system. Data were collected from 31 nonsyndromic UCLP patients who received comprehensive orthodontic treatment at a high-volume cleft center in Brazil. Patients were selected based on strict inclusion criteria, namely the availability of high- resolution pre -treatment and post -treatment digital dental models along with corresponding panoramic radiographs. The treatments were uniformly performed using conventional ﬁxed-appliance therapy, ensuring consistency in the treatment approach across the sample. Th e COR Scoring Grid A t the core of the COR system is a structured scoring grid that systematically evaluates a set of occlusal parameters (Table 1). The system focuses on static occlusion and includes: anteroposterior relationship assessed separately in the anterior and posterior segments; vertical relationship based on the presence or extent of positive/negative overbite or open bite in the anterior and posterior regions; transverse relationship evaluating edge-to-edge or buccal/lingual crossbites, weighted by severity and number of aﬀected teeth; alignment assessed

Each row of the grid corresponds to a particular occlusal characteristic. Parameters are scored on a scale from 0 to 4, with 0 indicating no deviation from ideal occlusion and 4 reﬂecting the most severe anomaly. In recent years, orthodontic therapy with clear aligners has been used for the treatment of a wide range of malocclusions [6]. Among the advantages of this therapy, there is a better quality of life during the treatment of patients [7] and a facilitation in the maneuvers of oral hygiene [8]. These characteristics of orthodontic therapy with clear aligners can be particularly important in patients who undergo long- term therapies, such as patients with CLP [2, 9]. Within this context, two main methodological approaches have become established for the quantitative analysis of the efficacy of clear aligners: traditional linear and angular measurements [10-17], and geometric morphometrics [18]. While linear and angular measurements are easily understood and applied in daily practice, they provide only a partial description of the overall movements, failing to fully capture the spatial relationships between different landmarks. Geometric morphometrics, on the other hand, analyze the shape of biological objects based on the coordinates of landmarks and allow for the separation of size and shape compon ents, offering a more comprehensive and sound description of morphological variations [19, 20]. The application of geometric morphometrics has proven particularly valuable in studying facial asymmetries and changes induced by growth or treatment in patients with craniofacial anomalies. Some movements can be classified as predictable with clear aligners; like distalization up to 2.5 mm, upper incisors retraction or expansion with molar inclination [13, 14, 17], but some others have been classified as not predictable, such as extrusion movements, rotation of cuspids, or bodily expansion [6]. To our knowledge, only one study has reported results on arch shape changes corroborating the possibility of clear aligners to produce symmetric arch shape changes [18]. Asymmetric changes have not been analyzed, as far as we are aware at this time. The aims of this study were to evaluate the predictability of tooth movements with clear aligners in CLP patients; and to assess the predictability of symmetric and asymmetric maxillary arch form changes induced by clear aligner therapy (CAT) in these patients. Six types of tooth movements were evaluated for each tooth from central incisor to second molar: m esio-distal, bucco-lingual, and vertical translations (in mm), and tip, torque, and rotation (in degrees). These movements were calculated in relation to the occlusal plane established at T0, following the methodology described by Huanca Ghislanzoni et al [15] and Castroflorio et al [10]. As described by these authors the analysis included only movements with translational prescriptions exceeding 0.5 mm and rotational prescriptions exceeding 2°. Th e lack of correction (LC) for each movement type was calculated as the difference between the PM and the AM. DISCUSSION The present study aimed to evaluate the predictability of tooth movements and arch form changes achieved with clear aligner therapy in a cohort of patients CLP . This patient population presents unique challenges due to inherent skeletal and dental characteristics, arch form alteration, and potential growth disturbances. Understanding the efficacy of clear aligners in these complex patients is crucial for optimizing treatment strategies and managing patient expectations [2, 9] . predictability of individual tooth movements reveal that, similar to non -cleft populations, clear aligners exhibit limitations in achieving certain prescribed movements with complete accuracy in CLP patients. The LC was statistically significant for a majority of movements across various tooth types when compared to clinically relevant thresholds (0.5 mm for translations, 2° for rotations). This aligns with the broader literature on clear aligner efficacy [6], which consistently reports discrepancies between planned and achieved outcomes . Specifically, lateral incisors demonstrated significant LC across most of the movement. This is a particularly relevant finding in CLP patients, as lateral incisors are frequently affected by the cleft, often being congenitally missing, peg -shaped, or malpositioned [24]. The high LC for torque and rotation of canines and premolars also aligns with findings in non-cleft samples [10-12], suggesting that the biomechanical limitations of applying rotational and torquing forces with aligners persist in the CLP context. This can be explained considering that most of the prescribed torque was to reduce torque; this is a predictable movement as shown by Wei and coworker [17]. The results of this study have several clinical implications for the orthodontic management of CLP patients with clear aligners. Clinicians should be aware of the movements that are less predictable (e.g., torque and rotation of canines and incisors, especially compromised lateral incisors) and incorporate appropriate overcorrections or plan for adjunctive techniques or refinements. The ability of clear aligners to effect changes in both symmetric and asymmetric aspects of arch form is promising. Expansion with retraction is a highly predictable movement. However, the incomplete achievement of planned outcomes suggests that for significant transverse discrepancies or asymmetries, aligners alone might be insufficient, or may require more extensive overcorrection and adjunctive therapies (e.g., miniscrew). Although a single experienced clinician treated all patients, variations in individual patient response and compliance could influence outcomes. The sample represents a specific treatment protoco l and aligner system; results might differ with other systems or protocols (e.g., different attachment strategies, aligner change intervals). The methodology used for superimposition has been validated in the literature, but the lack of fixed external reference points still decreases the reliability of the measurements. Future research should focus on prospective studies to further validate these findings and explore the influence of specific CLP characteristics (e.g., cleft type, severity, previous orthopedic treatment ) on aligner treatment predictability. Longitudinal studies assessing the stability of clear aligner outcomes in this population are also needed. CONCLUSIONS Clear aligner therapy can induce significant tooth movements and changes in maxillary arch form in patients with cleft lip and palate. However, similar to observations in non-cleft populations, discrepancies exist between planned and achieved outcomes. Cli nicians should consider these predictability patterns when planning treatments for patients with CLP, incorporating necessary overcorrections and anticipating the potential need for refinements or the use of auxiliaries to achieve optimal results. Preformed materials Preformed provisional crowns or matrices usually consist of tooth-shaped shells of plastic, cellulose ace- tate, or metal. They are commonly relined with acrylic resin to provide a more custom ﬁt before cementation, but the plastic and metal crown shells can also be ce- mented directly onto prepared teeth using a stiff luting material following adjustment. 14 They are commercially available in various tooth sizes and are usually selected for a particular tooth anatomy. Nonetheless, available sizes and contours are ﬁnite which makes the selection process important for clinical success. Compared with custom fabricated restorations, this treatment method is quick to perform but is more subject to abuse and inad- equate treatment outcome. SUMMARY The topic of provisional ﬁxed prosthodontic treat- ment involves a multifaceted array of clinical activities, special knowledge, material selection, and management. Contemporary treatment incorporates both natural teeth and dental implants. This

reat- ment involves a multifaceted array of clinical activities, special knowledge, material selection, and management. Contemporary treatment incorporates both natural teeth and dental implants. This literature review pro- vides a comprehensive summary of published reports on this topic. It characterizes clinical methods and provides clinicians with an understanding of the nature of mate- rials used with this clinical activity. Dentistry continues to struggle with the limitations of existing materials available for ﬁxed prosthodontic provisional treatment. Clinical techniques and indica- tions are reasonably well characterized, but future re- search activities will need to focus on technological ad- vancements to provide improved materials that demonstrate improved biocompatibility, ease of use and modiﬁcation, and physical properties. chunks.content: Functional orthopedics: The ‘tfour pieces” and Class II treatment M. Chateau,* H. Petit,** M. Roche,*** and W. Craig** Paris and Marseille, France, and Dallas, Texas The authors describe a new functional appliance called the Chateau four pieces, which is designed for the orthopedic treatment of Class II problems during growth. The versatility of the use of the four pieces, simultaneously or separately, enables the practitioner to control treatment in three dimensions. The indications and the prescription are discussed, and the results are shown. Key words: Dentofacial orthopedics, functional appliances, Class II T he purpose of this article is to familiarize the practitioner with a new dentofacial orthopedic appliance designed by Dr. Michel Chateau in France and currently used at Baylor College of Dentistry in Dallas, Texas. It presents some unique features which enable one to control the orthopedic results in three dimensions. As such, it is considered a functional appliance and a

As such, it is considered a functional appliance and a tridimensional activator. Activators, which evolved from the French monobloc (Robin, 1902-1905) are very popular at present. Their design looks quite simple but, in fact, there are some inherent difficulties in the management of both new activators and the earlier monoblocs. This is due to the complex- ity of a tridimensional control and the need for com- prehensive teaching. The situation can result in numer- ous failures. The “four pieces” appliance is designed to produce at least similar therapeutic potentialities with some im- portant additional ones. Even though it may look more complex at first glance, there is an obvious relationship between each “working piece” of the appliance and its tridimensional effect in space. Now, being familiar with the third and fourth pieces, we may return to the first piece, which is the maxillary plate (Fig. 2). The first piece The first piece is a regular palatal plate equipped essentially with two Adams clasps on the first perma- nent molars. A labial bow helps stabilize the appliance in the mouth and also can be used for correction of the labioversion of the upper incisors and for correction of the incisal rotations. Four tubes are embedded in the acrylic of the first piece in order to provide a convenient means of inser- tion of the third and fourth pieces. These tubes are oriented anteroposteriorly and obstructed distally to block the inserted pieces in a precise place. Moreover, the palatal plate is always split with a medial jack-

Moreover, the palatal plate is always split with a medial jack- screw. The reason for this is that, with correction of the Class II relationships, the teeth of the lower arch will occlude with a more anterior area of the upper arch and, therefore, at a narrower transversal dimension of the upper arch. Consequently, it is important to expand the upper arch in order to maintain compatibility within the two arches. 411 A nchorage has long been one of the greatest problems in the field of orthodontics because teeth, even molars, move in response to orthodontic forces. Therefore, in maximal anchorage cases, patients have needed to wear headgear. Thus reinforced anchorage with extraoral appliances has severe limitations because it requires excellent patient compliance. In the intermaxillary fixation after jaw surgery, maxillo - facial surgeons have also found that teeth do not make reli - able anchor units. T o solve this problem, surgeons proposed “skeletal anchorage” as an adjunct to tooth-borne anchorage. The maxillary teeth and bone were fixed with wires from the anterior nasal spine (ANS), infraorbital rim, or zygomatic arch. The mandibular teeth were anchored to the mandible with wires that circled the mandibular body in the anterior and posterior regions. In 1983 Creekmore and Eklund 1 reported a severe deep bite case that was successfully treated with a surgical vital - lium bone screw

circled the mandibular body in the anterior and posterior regions. In 1983 Creekmore and Eklund 1 reported a severe deep bite case that was successfully treated with a surgical vital - lium bone screw inserted just below the ANS to intrude the upper incisors. This was the first clinical report of “skeletal anchorage” for orthodontic tooth movement. A second case was reported by Jenner and Fitzpatrick 2 in 1985. They applied a large bone plate in the ramus to tip the mandibular molar distally with a leading wire and elastics. Our research group noted that the osteosynthesis tita - nium mini-plate had been thoroughly evaluated as an excel- lent biocompatible material in the field of maxillofacial surgery. In 1992 we developed the skeletal anchorage system (SAS) using titanium mini-plates 3 and, since then, SAS mechanics have been applied to various types of malocclu - sions in daily orthodontic practice. The advantages and disadvantages of the SAS are listed in Boxes 20-1 and 20-2. This

NEW ORTHODONTIC ANCHOR PLATES Because osteosynthesis titanium mini-plates were not de - signed as orthodontic anchor plates and are not necessarily suitable for orthodontic treatment, they were noted to have the following shortcomings: • Th e shape of the mini-plate is not suitable for the applica - tion of orthodontic force. • Th e surface of the arm portion that penetrates the muco - periosteum is roughly sandblasted and difficult to clean. • Th e size of the mini-plate is relatively thick and large. T o solve those problems, our research group developed the new orthodontic anchor plates. 4 Features Figure 20-1 shows the newly developed anchor plates, which are called

T o solve those problems, our research group developed the new orthodontic anchor plates. 4 Features Figure 20-1 shows the newly developed anchor plates, which are called SMAP (Super Mini Anchor Plate®, Dentsply- Sankin, T okyo, Japan). These plates are made of pure tita - nium, which is suitable for osseointegration and also tissue integration. In addition, Class II pure titanium is used, which is strong enough to withstand the usual orthodontic forces but can also be bent with ease for fitting into the bone contour of the implantation site. Figure 20-2 shows an example of the T-type anchor plate. The anchor plate consists of three portions: head, arm, and body. The head portion is intraorally exposed and positioned outside the dentition so that it never disturbs any kind of tooth movement. Each head portion has three continuous hooks for easier application of orthodontic forces. As the need arises, it is possible to cut off the first and second hooks.

There are two types of head portion, which differ with regard to the direction of hooks, and which type is used depends on the manner of tooth movement. The arm portion is transmucosal and has three graduated lengths—short (10.5-mm), medium (13.5-mm), and long (16.5-mm)—to compensate for individual morphological differences and to accommodate the manner of tooth move- ment (Fig. 20-3). 442 I n recent years, a trend toward implementing treatment plans that achieve rapid facial change has arisen. 1–5 In the surgery first (SF) treatment plan, the presurgical orthodontic treatment phase is completely eliminated, the jaws are surgically repositioned to the desired locations, and orthodontic tooth movement follows. Caution is impor- tant when embarking on SF treatment. Even a highly expe- rienced orthodontist/surgeon will not necessarily find it easy to identify the occlusal relationship that will accompany an ideal facial and functional result. This explains why numerous orthodontists prefer to conduct an orthodontic preparation before surgery. Having a stable postoperative occlusion is thought to be important for maintaining the bony stability. 5 The advent of temporary anchorage devices (TADs), including skeletal anchorage, was a breakthrough in achiev- ing teeth movement beyond traditional orthodontics. The skeletal anchorage system (SAS), which uses titanium mini-

anchorage devices (TADs), including skeletal anchorage, was a breakthrough in achiev- ing teeth movement beyond traditional orthodontics. The skeletal anchorage system (SAS), which uses titanium mini- plates to control moving teeth in nongrowing patients, has shown that it is possible to achieve predictable three- dimensional movement of teeth and entire dentition with fewer bicuspid extractions. 6,7 Contemplating SF treatment with the SAS began in 2003 at T ohoku University in Sendai, Japan. The distinguishing feature of this approach is an orthodontics-driven method referred to as Sendai SF . The surgery aims to first correct the skeletal deformity and then the SAS mini-plates, which are placed at the time of orthognathic surgery, manage the den- toalveolar problems and establish the functional and esthetic occlusion postsurgically. The fundamental concept of Sendai SF is to maintain the quality results seen in traditional surgi- cal orthodontics by making a precise prediction of

functional and esthetic occlusion postsurgically. The fundamental concept of Sendai SF is to maintain the quality results seen in traditional surgi- cal orthodontics by making a precise prediction of the final outcomes of both orthodontic and surgical correction prior to treatment. This chapter describes and illustrates the step-by-step protocol used in Sendai SF through four case examples. SENDAI SURGERY FIRST PROTOCOL The Sendai SF protocol has 15 steps (Box 22-1). Among these are four major steps, each of which is discussed below and illustrated with a detailed patient case example. Step 3: Orthognathic Surgery Accurate surgical technique has a major role in the success of Sendai SF . Achieving an appropriate osteotomy design, splitting, fixation technique, and proper condyle seating are key in conferring stable results. The surgeons on the Sendai SF team use a modified design of a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) combined with a T-shaped bone mini-plate fixation. 14–16 The design has a buccal step laid adjacent to the mandibular second molar area. This design prevents condylar dislocation and therefore minimizes relapse (Fig. 22-6). FUTURE OF SENDAI SF With recent developments in cone beam computed tomog - raphy (CBCT), virtual model surgery, model visual scan and setup, and wafer fabrication for orthognathic surgery, 29,30 Sendai SF can become a more accurate and predictable pro- cedure than the current state of care. At the same time, Sendai SF remains a new concept in surgical-orthodontic treatment. Further studies on the prediction of treatment goals and long-term stability are necessary. The increased level of cooperation between clinicians is very promising for implementing this technique, as the future of orthognathic surgery is geared toward minimizing overall treatment time without compromising the final results. ARY Recently, more attention has been given to the SF approach.1–5,7,28,31,32 One of the most challenging consider - ations in the SF technique is that it is a complicated approach that requires close cooperation between a highly experi - enced orthodontist and a surgeon. Prediction of the desired final occlusion is not easy. This chapter explained the Sendai SF technique step-by-step, including the planning process and application. It should be noted that the severity of a malocclusion is an important factor in determining the length of treatment time. Patients with mildly crowded teeth will have a shorter treatment time compared to patients with severely crowded teeth. In the patient described throughout the chapter, the orthodontic work took nearly 10 months and the total treatment time was 11 months. She was classified as having a moderately crowded occlusion. The authors have experienced longer treatment times in patients with severely crowded occlusions (see Case Reports 1 to

time was 11 months. She was classified as having a moderately crowded occlusion. The authors have experienced longer treatment times in patients with severely crowded occlusions (see Case Reports 1 to 3). Regardless, the treatment time remains significantly shorter than what might be experienced with conventional orthodontic/ orthognathic surgery. 20 Among the benefits of the Sendai SF approach are a greatly reduced treatment time, the rapid improvement of the patient’ s profile, and the quick improvement of the patient’ s quality of life. It is the authors’ belief that these benefits significantly outweigh the potential problems asso - ciated with Sendai SF and that this innovative treatment approach may soon become a standard clinical option. 474 W hen using orthognathic surgery, application of appropriate diagnosis, treatment planning, bio - mechanical principles, surgical technique, and timing are all necessary to optimize individual patient treat- ment outcomes. From the discipline’ s inception in the mid- nineteenth century through its peak in the 1980s and its continued evolution in the early 2000s, advances have been made in both diagnostic and treatment-related areas. Initial updates made orthognathic surgery a safer and more practi- cal treatment alternative with the development of antibiotics, enhanced surgical techniques, and later rigid fixation. The improved surgical techniques enabled orthodontists to rethink the timing and type of surgical preparation and ulti- mately enabled orthognathic surgery to become increasingly predictable, with dramatic facial and occlusal improvement the normal outcome. More recently, diagnostic advances such as cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) and computer aided surgical

increasingly predictable, with dramatic facial and occlusal improvement the normal outcome. More recently, diagnostic advances such as cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) and computer aided surgical simulation (CASS) offer tremendous value and new plan - ning opportunities to the orthodontist, the oral and maxil - lofacial surgeon, and their patients. Both techniques now enable the care team to truly understand the three- dimensional (3D) nature of patient jaw deformities to better simulate and plan treatment before undertaking care. While planning is essential, the greater benefit is the “failure analy- sis” from the 3D images, which enhances future patient care by preventing adverse outcomes. Advances have not been restricted to the planning phase but have also included the development of new treatments such as distraction osteogenesis, surgery for the obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) patient, mandibular constriction, earlier surgical intervention, and skeletal anchorage with

velopment of new treatments such as distraction osteogenesis, surgery for the obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) patient, mandibular constriction, earlier surgical intervention, and skeletal anchorage with temporary anchorage devices (TADs) used before, during, and follow - ing surgery, each of which potentially alter the biomechani- cal approach and surgical intervention planned for the patient. While distraction osteogenesis is unlikely to replace traditional orthognathic surgery because, for example, it cannot be used in cases of excessive jaw growth, it offers a treatment alternative for correction of skeletal jaw deficien - cies. Unfortunately, few papers describe the detailed biome- chanical approach necessary to achieve the correct vectors and movements for optimal treatment results. Orthodontic appliance and TAD placement, localizing the center of resis- tance of the osteotomized segments, and location of force application are vitally important to minimize treatment complications

Orthodontic appliance and TAD placement, localizing the center of resis- tance of the osteotomized segments, and location of force application are vitally important to minimize treatment complications and enhance treatment outcomes. The same efficient, effective, operator-determined biomechanical prin- ciples necessary to produce excellent orthodontic outcomes must be applied to both distraction osteogenesis and TADs. The biomechanical principles are the same whether focusing on tooth-to-tooth movement or bony segment–to–bony segment movement yet few recognize the merging of these disciplines. Logical, sequential, and appropriate application of these and other related updates and their impact on diagnosis, treatment planning, surgical considerations, methods of effi- cient leveling, arch coordination, space closure, and other aspects of orthodontic mechanotherapy are discussed in this chapter. 205 N onextraction treatment has gained in popularity in the orthodontic community since the second half of the twentieth century. This is due to the paradigm shift from focusing on the dentition to appraising the whole face. The careful selection of patients and timing of treat- ment are essential to the success of nonextraction treatment. When planning nonextraction treatment, we opt to use early treatment, redirection of growth, saving leeway space, guid- ance of eruption, and mechanics that aim to achieve distal movement of the maxillary molars. For a successful outcome, it is necessary before the initiation of treatment to take into consideration the type of malocclusion, facial type, required arch perimeter, individual growth, and motivation of the patient. Class II, Division 1 malocclusion has been described as the most frequent treatment problem in orthodontic prac- tice. It is estimated that about 35% of American children have Class II malocclusions. alocclusion has been described as the most frequent treatment problem in orthodontic prac- tice. It is estimated that about 35% of American children have Class II malocclusions. Distal movement of the maxil - lary first molars is a common goal in the treatment of the Class II molar relationship and in the resolution of tooth size–arch length discrepancy in the maxillary arch. Early treatment is the key to successful treatment of Class II malocclusions. During the 1940s and 1950s Kloehn 1 sug- gested the use of headgear during the transitional dentition to correct molar relations. In the 1960s Ricketts et a l.2 pro- moted the bioprogressive philosophy, which used utility arches, quad helix, and cervical facebow headgear among several other innovative appliance systems. However, the real impetus behind nonextraction treatment was the realization that for far too long orthodontists had focused on the place- ment of the denture on the basal bone without sufficient regard to the facial

Research findings on long- term retention of treated dentitions revealed that relapse was common in both extraction and nonextraction treatment modalities. Cetlin and T en Hoeve 3 showed stable results for nonextraction treatment of patients with severe malocclu- sions. The thickness of facial soft tissue integument varies among individuals and its growth pattern is specific to indi- viduals throughout their lifespan and not just during the period of active growth.4 In view of these findings, the non - extraction treatment modality has become a treatment of choice for select groups of patients. Bimetric (Wilson) Arch Wilson24 introduced the bimetric arch into the orthodontic literature in 1955 at a time when there was considerable argument between proponents of extraction and of nonex - traction with expansion. The appliance consists of a labial arch made of a 0.040-inch posterior section and a 0.020-inch anterior section. Hooks for Class II elastics are soldered onto the anterior end of the 0.040-inch section and an adjustable omega loop is placed in the premolar region of the 0.040- inch section. Jones Jig Appliance The Jones jig appliance43 is an intraoral noncompliance dis - talization appliance (Fig. 12-11). It has a modified Nance appliance banded to the second bicuspids, with the Jones jig assemblies tied in place. The majority of the studies on this appliance have shown that Class II correction is attributed to a slight increase in mandibular length, a significant posterior movement of the maxillary posterior segments, and proclination of the lower incisors. 52,53 SUMMARY Headgear is perhaps the most useful appliance for maxillary molar distalization if used in the early treatment of Class II malocclusions. Kim et a l.5 have shown that the occlusion established early during the growth phase is most likely to be maintained throughout life. Based on this and the premise that children are more compliant before adolescence, the headgear becomes a versatile appliance for treatment of Class II malocclusions. Its effect is twofold: (1) distal move - ment of the maxillary molars and (2) an orthopedic effect on the maxilla that restrains growth. Both extraoral and intraoral inter-arch appliances require patient

Both extraoral and intraoral inter-arch appliances require patient compliance, which may sometimes pose difficulty. Intermaxillary appliances that use the mandibular arch as anchorage may have protrusive effects on the mandibular teeth. All investigations that have evaluated intraoral arch noncompliance appliances for molar distalization have come to surprisingly similar conclusions on the behavior of both the distal segment and the anterior anchor unit. The intra - maxillary arch appliances, which have gained in popularity because they do not require patient compliance to distalize molars, show loss of anchorage whereby the premolars move mesially with concomitant protrusion of the maxillary inci - sors. 74 T he physical concepts that form the foundation of orthodontic mechanics are the key to understanding how orthodontic appliances work and are critical in designing treatment methodologies and appliances. These physical concepts are not unique to orthodontics but are the elementary laws of mechanics in general. In this chapter we outline the ground rules and fundamentals that guide orth - odontic tooth movement. All appliance systems reported in the past and all systems that will be reported in the future will use these principles of mechanics. However, let us start from the beginning: What does the word “mechanics” mean? Mechanics can be defined as a branch of physics con - cerned with the mechanical aspects of any system. This can be divided into two categories: statics, the study of factors associated with nonmoving (rigid) systems, and dynamics, the study of factors associated with systems in motion, such as a moving car or a plane. When the knowledge and meth - ods of mechanics

factors associated with nonmoving (rigid) systems, and dynamics, the study of factors associated with systems in motion, such as a moving car or a plane. When the knowledge and meth - ods of mechanics are applied to the structure and function of living systems (biology)—for example, a tooth and its sur- rounding oral architecture—it is called biomechanics. It is our belief that the study of biomechanics of tooth movement can help researchers and clinicians to optimize their force systems applied on teeth to get better responses at the clini - cal, tissue, cellular, or molecular level of tooth movement. APPROACHES TO STUDYING TOOTH MOVEMENT Two approaches are used to study the biological and me- chanical aspects of tooth movement: a quantitative approach and a qualitative approach. The quantitative approach in- volves describing movement of teeth or the associated skel - etal structures in numerical terms. W e all are familiar with terms such as 3-mm of canine retraction or 15 degrees

antitative approach in- volves describing movement of teeth or the associated skel - etal structures in numerical terms. W e all are familiar with terms such as 3-mm of canine retraction or 15 degrees of incisor flaring. Merely describing tooth movement quantita- tively does not describe the complete nature of the move - ment. It is also important to understand the type or nature of tooth movement that has occurred. A qualitative approach describes movement in nonnumerical terms (i.e., without measuring or counting any parts of the performance). This approach is often followed at the clinical level or inferred from x-rays and/or stone models such as tipping and translation. Both qualitative and quantitative analyses provide valu - able information about a performance. However, a quali - tative assessment is the predominant method used by orthodontists to analyze tooth movement. A system is a body or group of bodies or objects whose motion is to be examined; it might be a ball, a car, or a tooth. W e also need to identify a frame of reference within which a system’ s movement takes place. This can be either the stationary environment or something that is also moving. CENTER OF RESISTANCE, CENTER OF GRAVITY, AND CENTER OF MASS Once a force is applied to a body, its nature of motion is regulated to a large extent by its center of mass. The center of mass of a body may be thought of as that point at which all of the body’ s mass seems to be concentrated (i.e., if a force is applied through this point, the system or body will move in a straight line). On similar lines recall that the earth exerts a force on each segment of a system in direct proportion to each segment’ s mass. The total effect of the force of gravity on a whole body, or system, is as if the force of gravity were concentrated at a single point called the center of gravity. The difference between the center of mass and the center of gravity is that the system in question in the latter is a “restrained system” (restrained by the force of gravity). Therefore statics is that branch of physics that deals with the mechanics of nonaccelerating objects or, for our convenience and understanding, “nonmoving” objects. Such a system is said to be in equilibrium. T o achieve equilibrium, we must see to it that no unbalanced force is applied to the body in question or, in other words, that any force acting on a system is balanced by contrary forces. Therefore the sum of all forces should be zero (ΣF = 0). (According to Newton’ s Second Law of Motion, if a system is not accelerating, then a = 0, so ΣF = ma or ΣF = m(0) or ΣF = 0. 108 T ooth movement to close space is one of the most desired goals of orthodontic treatment. For years, orthodontists have searched for an efficient force system that can work quickly, accurately, and effectively to close extraction spaces. Orthodontic tooth movement is the result of the controlled application of mechanical forces to the teeth and periodontium. The stimulus provided by activated orthodontic appliances provides the necessary mechanical force to elicit a biological response. This pertur - bation temporarily disrupts the physiological equilibrium of the dentofacial complex and causes tooth movement in the direction of the net force, resulting in the closure of space. T o carry out such movements, orthodontic tools should be chosen on the basis of the biological responses of the periodontium surrounding the teeth (not yet an exact science) and their biomechanical properties as well as the appliances being used to move them (a much more exact science), rather than on the

Depending on the needs of the patient, one set of teeth or one tooth can be classified as the active unit while the other is classified as the passive or reactive unit. These two units have completely different roles during tooth movement. The active unit undergoes the majority of the movement while the passive unit resists any kind of movement and provides the resistance necessary to facilitate the movement of the active unit, thereby serving as an anchorage. An implicit advantage of canine retraction on a continuous arch system lies in limiting the possibility of unpredicted canine movement (e.g., flaring or rotation). Despite the advantages of sliding mechanics, canine retraction does present its own set of problems.
